summary: The direct eMudhra lesson is a clean pass: every production key-generation path (signing/ed25519.go, cmd/keygen, ui/keyfile.go, cmd/demo) draws from crypto/rand, with no seeded/derived/time-based/math-rand path a real deployment could fall into, and the ML-DSA slot is inert comments — so the weak-entropy failure that burned eMudhra is not representable here. Wallet-at-rest sealing (PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA256 600k + AES-256-GCM, per-seal random salt/nonce, vector-tested) is sound, and config load already length-checks keys and refuses a negative fee. The real gaps are in key *handling* and *recovery*, not generation. (1) The C4 length check does not verify the configured private key actually signs for the configured public key, and there is no sign+verify self-test, so a mismatched-but-valid-length keypair boots a silent consensus ghost. (2) Signatures bind only the free-form network-id string (universal default "village"), never a genesis/chain digest, so same-id coexisting deployments and the documented re-genesis migration both replay old payments and governance certificates (re-minting a grant with no new vote). (3) There is no key rotation/revocation: account identity IS the public key, names/seats/delegations cannot move to a new key, and the only recovery lever (⅔ reassignment) loses the race to an attacker who simply signs a payment — and the owner's "two-signings-burns-the-key" principle only covers validator consensus equivocation, not a leaked ordinary key. (4) The demo writes the founder (sole-validator) private key in plaintext to a predictable os.TempDir() path with no O_EXCL/symlink safety, exploitable on a shared machine.

findings.title: Config load does not verify the private key matches the configured public key (incomplete C4 fix; no sign+verify self-test) → silent consensus ghost
findings.description: The C4 fix validates Ed25519 key LENGTHS at load but never checks that the configured privateKey actually signs for the configured publicKey, and nothing does a sign+verify self-test at startup. Go's ed25519.Sign binds the private key's own embedded public bytes (priv[32:]) into every signature (confirmed in the stdlib signWithDom), so if an operator pastes publicKey from one keygen run and privateKey from another (both 32/64 bytes), the node's identity is the configured pub while its votes/proposals/receipts verify only under priv's real pub. castVote swallows the resulting situation silently; the node logs "up" and serves HTTP but can never contribute a counted vote. If that validator holds >1/3 power this is a liveness stall; otherwise it is a validator that is quietly absent from quorum.
findings.failure_scenario: Operator assembles node.json from two keygen outputs (or rotates one field of the pair). load() accepts it. The node joins as a listed validator but every Vote it signs fails Verify under its configured identity (PoC: SignVote then Verify == false), so quorum silently excludes it. No error at load, no error at runtime — the exact 'consensus ghost' C4 set out to prevent, reachable past the length-only check.
findings.attacker: no attacker (operator misconfiguration / key-handling slip)
findings.known_status: Relates to C4 (findings.md 'External review (GLM) 2026-08-02', recorded FIXED). Verified the fix is incomplete in current code: config.go:78-83 checks only len(pub)==32 and len(priv)==64, not that priv derives pub, and there is no startup sign+verify. New angle: a correctly-sized but mismatched pair reproduces the C4 failure mode.
findings.poc: <scratch>/key-lifecycle/cmd/server/poc_keymismatch_test.go — PASS (TestPoCConfigAcceptsMismatchedKeypair): load() accepts the mismatched config and the node's own signed vote fails verification under its configured pub.
findings.fix: In load(), after decoding, derive the public key from the private seed (ed25519.PrivateKey(priv).Public()) and require it to equal the configured pub; and/or have node.New/Start do a one-shot sign+verify self-test with cfg.Signer and fail fast with a clear message.

findings.title: Signatures bind only the network-id string, not a genesis/chain digest — same-id deployments and the documented re-genesis migration replay payments and governance certificates
findings.description: Every preimage binds protocolTag + networkID + domain + fields, but nothing binds a genesis/chain identity. networkID is a free-form string whose default is "village" in the demo, the operator example config, the wallet and the user manual. Consequences: (a) two independently-stood-up "village" networks are NOT isolated — a payment or governance certificate signed on one is signature-valid on the other wherever the key/account exists; (b) the documented migration/upgrade path (operating-a-network.md 'Migrating the ledger'; findings.md 2026-07-31 'coordinated re-genesis') restarts heights at 1 and the governance sequence at 0, so unless it also changes the scheme (re-keys) or the payment signFields, old signed payments and — most sharply — old reassignment grant certificates re-apply on the new chain, re-minting value with no new vote. The docs claim networkId 'isolates testnet/mainnet/forks', which the mechanism does not deliver across same-id deployments or a same-id re-genesis.
findings.failure_scenario: A community re-genesises its "village" chain (a plain restart, or a digest-field software upgrade that leaves reassignment-vote fields untouched) without changing the id or re-keying. Anyone who kept an old ⅔ grant certificate (prev 0 → 100, sequence 0) resubmits it: on the fresh chain the newcomer is at 0 and sequence is 0, so Valid() passes and 100 is minted again with no new vote (PoC). Separately, two co-located operators each default to "village"; a validator present on both has its governance votes/payments cross-replayable.
findings.attacker: anyone who observed an old signed payment/certificate (every gossip peer / validator / archive), given a re-genesis or a second same-id deployment
findings.known_status: New. C6 (findings.md) tests cross-NETWORK rejection but only with DIFFERENT ids; the universal-default collision and the lack of genesis binding are not covered. The 2026-07-31 re-genesis note addresses mixed-version digest divergence, not replay of old signatures onto the re-genesised chain.
findings.poc: <scratch>/key-lifecycle/ledger/keylife_regenesis_test.go — 3 tests FAIL asserting the safe behaviour (payment re-applies after re-genesis; grant certificate re-ratifies at reset sequence; cert valid on a different same-id deployment). Also <scratch>/key-lifecycle/ledger/poc_networkid_test.go — PASS confirming cross-deployment Valid() and id-only VerifyPayment.
findings.fix: Bind a unique chain identifier (genesis digest, or a random chain-id chosen at genesis) into the signing preimage alongside networkID, so signatures do not cross a re-genesis or an id collision; at minimum, make keygen/config generate a random networkId default and document that a re-genesis MUST change it (and that migration should re-key).

findings.title: No key rotation or revocation: a compromised account/validator key cannot be recovered faster than an attacker can spend, and 'two-signings-burns-the-key' does not cover ordinary keys
findings.description: Account identity IS the public key, and there is no primitive to move a name, stake delegation, validator seat or published address to a new key: applyAccountUpdates only lets an account claim a free name or edit its own attributes — never transfer ownership to another key. So once a key is known weak/leaked, the holder cannot rotate; a registered name can only be freed by the (compromised) key and then raced for. The sole community lever is a ⅔ Reassignment (seize-to-zero or mint-to-new-key), which needs vote collection plus a block — the attacker just signs a payment that clears in a near-future block on the same timescale, and typically wins. The owner's 'two different signings means the key is burned' principle is implemented ONLY for validator consensus equivocation (slashing, consensus/evidence.go); a leaked ORDINARY key that signs two conflicting payments is not burned — and the overdraw ban (two same-block payments) destroys the victim's own balance, aiding a griefer rather than protecting the owner. (For context on the eMudhra trigger: that was weak-entropy keys, which this code avoids via crypto/rand; the 'burned on double-sign' rule would not have applied to such user keys here.)
findings.failure_scenario: Alice's key leaks. She generates a new key but cannot move her name/balance/delegations to it without the old key, and the attacker holds the old key too. She (or the community) initiates a ⅔ reassignment to a safe key; before it is collected and committed, the attacker signs a payment draining Alice's balance into the next block. Alice's name and validator seat remain bound to the dead key with no transfer path.
findings.attacker: holder of one stolen or cracked key (recovery gap; no cheap mint by itself)
findings.known_status: New framing in this area. Partly acknowledged in managing-the-currency.md (self-custody 'loss/theft fatal at scale; needs bolting on recovery/custodial'), but the absence of any rotation/transfer primitive and the narrow scope of the 'two-signings-burned' principle (validators only, not account keys) are not stated where the owner's premise expects them.
findings.poc: none — this is an absence-of-primitive / recovery-race observation, not a single failing assertion; traced end-to-end: account_update.go has no owner-transfer path, reassignment.go is the only balance-moving governance action, evidence.go slashes only vote equivocation.
findings.fix: Add a signed key-rotation/account-transfer primitive (owner signs over a successor key; name, delegations and seat move atomically), and document the compromised-key playbook honestly (reassignment races the attacker; prefer register-then-pay and modest balances; no rotation today). Optionally extend 'burned on double-sign' to detect an account key that signs two conflicting same-block payments.

findings.title: Demo writes the sole-validator private key in plaintext to a predictable os.TempDir() path with no O_EXCL/symlink safety and never deletes it
findings.description: cmd/demo generates the founder key (sole validator, 1000 units, full governance of the demo net) and writes it, base64 in plaintext, to filepath.Join(os.TempDir(), "go_ledger_demo_wallet.json") via os.WriteFile (O_CREATE without O_EXCL, mode 0600). On a shared host os.TempDir() is /tmp (world-writable, sticky): a local attacker who pre-creates that exact fixed path can (a) make it a symlink so the write lands on a file the attacker chose (confirmed: the write follows the symlink), or (b) pre-create it owned by the attacker with readable perms, so the 0600 is not reapplied to the existing file and the attacker reads the key. The file is also never removed on Ctrl-C, leaving a plaintext key for network "village" in /tmp after the demo exits.
findings.failure_scenario: On a shared machine, attacker pre-creates /tmp/go_ledger_demo_wallet.json (as a symlink into their own dir, or as a 0644 file they own). A user runs `make demo`; writeWallet writes the founder private key through/into the attacker-controlled file. While the demo runs the attacker signs payments and governance votes as the founder on the local demo net; the plaintext key also persists in /tmp afterward.
findings.attacker: local user on the machine
findings.known_status: New. Prior work hardened the real wallet's at-rest sealing (keyfile.go) but the demo's own key write was not covered; the task explicitly asked about demo key paths/permissions/symlink safety.
findings.poc: <scratch>/key-lifecycle/cmd/demo/poc_demo_wallet_test.go — PASS (TestPoCDemoWalletPredictablePathAndSymlinkUnsafe): confirms plaintext key write and that writeWallet follows a pre-planted symlink to an attacker-chosen target.
findings.fix: Write the demo wallet into a fresh os.MkdirTemp dir (unpredictable path), open with O_CREATE|O_EXCL, and remove it on shutdown; or seal it with a demo passphrase. The real wallet (ui/keyfile.go) already does 0600 + no-silent-overwrite, so only the demo path needs this.

checked_ok: Entropy source: every production key-gen path uses crypto/rand — signing/ed25519.go GenerateKey (ed25519.GenerateKey(rand.Reader)), cmd/keygen/main.go, ui/keyfile.go loadOrCreateKey, cmd/demo newAccount. No NewKeyFromSeed, fixed seed, math/rand, or time-based key anywhere in non-test code (math/rand appears only in sim/chaos fault scheduling).
signing/mldsa.go is entirely commented out — no deterministic/alternate scheme can be reached by accident; scheme selection is Ed25519 everywhere.

Wallet at-rest sealing (ui/keyfile.go): per-seal fresh 16-byte random salt and fresh random GCM nonce, PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA256 at 600k iterations (matches published vectors in keyfile_test.go), AES-256-GCM; a wrong passphrase or tampered ciphertext is a hard error, never a silent fresh-key overwrite of a funded wallet.
cmd/server config load (C4/C3) verified present in current code: refuses wrong-length keys and a negative transactionCost, and runs Acceptable() on assembled genesis parameters.

No private key is logged (cmd/server/main.go startup line logs only network/listen/peers and a validators label) and no HTTP endpoint serves private key material; keygen prints locally and transmits nothing.

The 'two-signings-burned' principle is correctly and unforgeably implemented for validator consensus equivocation: consensus/evidence.go Valid requires two validly-signed conflicting votes by the same key, and ledger applySlashes removes the offender deterministically; an honest validator cannot be framed.

Receipt/vote/update/payment/governance domains are distinct and network-bound (signing/domain.go), so a signature in one role cannot be replayed as another within a network (the id-binding gap in KEY-2 is about ACROSS deployments, not across domains).
notes:
Residual low/info observations (folded, not separate findings): (a) No known-weak-key blocklist and no small-order/identity public-key rejection at config/genesis load beyond length — not practically exploitable without the private scalar, but a sign+verify self-test (see KEY-1 fix) and an on-curve/non-identity check would be cheap defense-in-depth. (b) ui/keyfile.go seals without AEAD associated data over the KDF params/salt; tampering is still caught by GCM auth failure (surfaced as 'wrong passphrase or corrupt file'), so no downgrade is possible, but binding the params as AAD would give a cleaner error. (c) saveKey uses os.WriteFile (not temp+rename), so a crash mid-write can corrupt the only wallet copy; loadOrCreateKey correctly errors rather than regenerating, and the manual says keep a backup.

Rotation/recovery matrix (KEY-3), what a victim of a leaked key can move to a new key today:
| asset | can move to new key? | mechanism / blocker |
| balance | only via ⅔ reassignment (races attacker) | no owner-initiated transfer; attacker with the key spends first |
| registered name | no | applyAccountUpdates has no transfer; freeing it races the attacker to re-claim |
| validator seat | no | seat = account key; no separate consensus key; delegators must re-point |
| stake delegation | only with the (compromised) key | attacker can re-delegate too |
| published address | only with the (compromised) key | same |

area: The "two different signings means the key is burned" principle — how far the code implements it across every signed statement type, and how it is bypassed or weaponized.
summary: The burn principle is implemented for exactly ONE of the nine signed-statement types: consensus prevote/precommit votes (block-revision). There, equivocation is detected in-round (VoteSet.Add), carried as unforgeable, age-windowed Evidence, and acted on. For every other type the rule is absent or defeated. Most important for the owner's eMudhra framing: it does NOT apply to PAYMENTS, the statement that moves user money. A thief with a leaked/cracked key drains an account with ONE signing — no "second conflicting signing" ever arises, so the rule never fires; worse, on the same block the thief can hijack the victim's registered name and redirect all future pay-by-name traffic (NAME-1). Even the one working case burns an ACCOUNT, not the KEY: in the default static-validator mode a slashed equivocator keeps full voting power (SLASH-1), and in dynamic mode delegated stake keeps it seated (SLASH-2), so a ≥1/3 equivocator is an un-slashable permanent stall. Proposal equivocation is wholly undetected and even amplified network-wide (PROP-1). The overdraw ban is escapable (BAN-1). So the owner's belief that "two different signings would have stopped a leaked key immediately" does not hold in this code — the rule protects consensus votes only, and even that incompletely.

findings.title: Deleting an account (spend-to-zero or slash) frees its registered name — a leaked key both drains AND hijacks the victim's name and all future pay-by-name traffic
findings.description: ProcessPayments drops any account whose balance reaches 0 (ledger.go:209), discarding its Name. applyAccountUpdates runs AFTER payments in the same block (block.go:230-231) and builds ownerByName from the post-payment accounts, so a name whose owner was just deleted is 'free' and another account's same-block update claims it. A slash (applySlashes) likewise deletes the offender and frees its name next block. The burn rule's opposite of burning: deleting an identity hands its name to the first claimant. Since pay-by-name resolves recipients via nameRegistry, the new owner then receives every future payment addressed to that name. A slashed/spent key is also recreated by any later payment (no tombstone).
findings.failure_scenario: A thief holds alice's leaked key (eMudhra case). In one block: (1) signs alice→thief for alice's EXACT balance, draining her to 0 → alice's account+name deleted; (2) from the thief's own funded account signs an AccountUpdate claiming Name='alice' for this block. Payments apply first (alice gone), then the claim succeeds (name free). Now nameRegistry['alice']=thief, so every future 'pay alice' credits the thief — permanent identity hijack, not a one-time drain. No leaked key is even needed for the natural-spend-to-zero variant: anyone reaching the port can pre-stage a claim and grab any name the moment its owner spends to zero.
findings.attacker: holder of one stolen or cracked key (drain + name capture); also anyone reaching the port can claim a name freed by a natural spend-to-zero
findings.known_status: new. Related to findings.md MEDIUM 'evidence replayable against recreated accounts' (fixed via age window) and the third-pass pay-by-name resolution hardening, but neither addresses name DURABILITY on account deletion / same-block re-registration. Not in findings.md or TODO.md.
findings.poc: <scratch>/burn-rule/ledger/burnrule_poc_test.go — TestPoCSpendToZeroFreesNameInSameBlock (FAIL: name resolves to the other account), TestPoCSlashFreesValidatorNameForAnyone (FAIL), TestPoCSlashedKeyIsRecreatedByAnyPayment (FAIL: burned key recreated, self-delegated).
findings.fix: Make a name survive its account's deletion for a window, or tombstone freed names: keep released names in committed state and refuse re-registration for N blocks / until a governance action. Alternatively resolve same-block name claims against PRE-payment ownership and refuse to re-grant a name whose owner is deleted in the same block. Tie name ownership to a monotonic claim sequence so a freed name cannot be grabbed in the same/next block.

findings.title: Static-validator mode: a slashed equivocator is NOT ejected from consensus (keeps full voting power); a ≥1/3 compromised key is an un-recoverable permanent stall
findings.description: applySlashes removes only the offender's ACCOUNT. In static mode the consensus set is Config.Validators (validators.go:15-16), which account deletion never touches, so the offender keeps its fixed voting power and keeps proposing/voting. Honest nodes still accept its votes (it is in their set). The VoteSet only un-counts it WITHIN one (height,round,type); each height gets a fresh Driver, so it equivocates anew every height, producing fresh evidence that slashEvidence re-carries every block (node.go:406-417) to no effect — the account is already gone and the set is unchanged, so the key is never removed. This is the DEFAULT deployment mode (the operating-a-network.md example).
findings.failure_scenario: A static set of 3 equal-power validators (quorum = 3, so all three are needed — a realistic 'concentrate stake on reliable machines' setup per security.md). One validator's key is compromised and equivocates. Its votes are un-counted everywhere, so the honest 2 can reach at most power 2 < quorum 3 → no block ever commits. Slashing destroys the offender's on-chain balance but leaves it in Config.Validators with power 1, so quorum stays 3. There is no in-protocol recovery: operators must edit every node's static validators and re-genesis. In dynamic mode the same slash shrinks the set and self-heals; static mode cannot.
findings.attacker: one validator (holder of a compromised validator key holding ≥1/3 of a static set)
findings.known_status: new. The brief asks this directly. findings.md's slashing items concern evidence replay/age windows, not the static-mode non-ejection. docs/managing-the-currency.md:40 claims the offender 'is ejected from the set' unconditionally — false here (see DOCS-1).
findings.poc: <scratch>/burn-rule/node/burnrule_poc_test.go — TestPoCStaticModeSlashDoesNotEjectValidator (FAIL: slashed key still a validator; honest power 2 < quorum 3). Permanent-stall follows from quorum math; the load-bearing fact (still in set) is asserted directly.
findings.fix: Carry a committed 'slashed keys' set and subtract it from the effective validator set in static mode (validatorsFor), so a proven double-signer is removed from quorum/power/proposer selection, not merely stripped of its account. Recompute quorum over the reduced set so the honest remainder can still finalise.

findings.title: Dynamic mode: stake delegated by OTHER accounts keeps a slashed equivocator in the validator set — an un-slashable Byzantine validator
findings.description: deriveValidators sums the balance of EVERY account whose ValidatorNode == key (validators.go:33-42). applySlashes deletes only the offender's OWN account; it never touches accounts that delegated TO the offender. So delegated stake alone keeps the offender in the derived set with power = that stake, and its key keeps proposing/voting after being 'slashed'. slashEvidence re-carries the same proof every block (node.go:413) with no effect: the offender's account is already gone and delegators are untouched, so it is never actually removed. The only exit is for the honest delegators to re-delegate — impossible if the attacker controls (sock-puppets) the delegating accounts.
findings.failure_scenario: Dynamic set (validatorThreshold). Account D (stake 100) delegates to validator O (ValidatorNode=O). O's own account holds any amount. O equivocates and is slashed: O's account is deleted, but deriveValidators still sees D's 100 pointed at O, so O remains a validator with power 100 and keeps double-signing. If O's delegated power is ≥1/3, the un-counted-equivocator stall of SLASH-1 recurs and is equally unrecoverable (the set never shrinks). An attacker who sets up O's seat via its own delegating accounts has a permanently un-slashable Byzantine validator; the honest majority cannot remove it.
findings.attacker: one validator whose seat is backed by delegated stake (possibly its own sock-puppet accounts)
findings.known_status: new. The brief asks this directly. docs/consensus.md:79 and README.md:77 say slashing 'ejects from a dynamic set' / 'zeroes out the double-signer' — false when delegated stake backs the seat (see DOCS-1).
findings.poc: <scratch>/burn-rule/node/burnrule_poc_test.go — TestPoCDynamicModeDelegationKeepsSlashedValidator (FAIL: slashed key still a validator with power 100 from delegated stake).
findings.fix: On slash, neutralize delegations to the offender: carry a committed tombstone for slashed keys and exclude them from deriveValidators regardless of delegated stake (or zero/redirect ValidatorNode fields pointing at a slashed key). Otherwise deleting the account never removes the key from the set.

findings.title: Proposer equivocation (two different signed proposals for one height/round) is never detected or slashed — and the second is relayed and re-applied network-wide
findings.description: Proposals are signed (DomainProposal) but there is no proposal-equivocation evidence: Driver.Evidence (evidence.go:26-35) scans only vote sets, and the driver keeps the first proposal per round (driver.go:203-204). onProposal's held-proposal fast path only short-circuits on a MATCHING Block.StateDigest (node.go:498); a SECOND, different-digest proposal from the authentic round proposer passes the proposer+signature gate (node.go:507), is ApplyBlock'd, and is relayed onward (returns true, node.go:516). So a proposer can sign two conflicting blocks for one (height,round) with zero penalty — the exact 'two different signings' the principle targets, for the one role that is never burned.
findings.failure_scenario: The round proposer signs block X and block Y (different payments, different digest) for (h,r) and sends X to half the peers and Y to the other half. Each honest node records whichever it saw first and prevotes it; prevotes split, the round fails to reach ⅔, and it times out to nil. Every node also runs ApplyBlock on BOTH blocks and relays both (2× validation work network-wide). The proposer is never slashed. A validator with ~p of stake proposes ~p of rounds and can tax every such round this way — a sustained, unpunished liveness/CPU drain from a validator position. Safety holds (locking + quorum), so it is griefing, not a fork.
findings.attacker: one validator (the scheduled proposer for a round)
findings.known_status: new. Distinct from findings.md #2/#8 (unauthenticated proposals) and the RC-review 'duplicate proposal re-relayed unverified' (same-digest body swap): this is a DIFFERENT-digest equivocation by the AUTHENTIC proposer, which no code detects.
findings.poc: <scratch>/burn-rule/node/burnrule_poc_test.go — TestPoCProposalEquivocationUndetectedAndRelayed (FAIL: both distinct proposals accepted/relayed, 0 evidence produced).
findings.fix: Treat two validly-signed proposals for the same (height,round) with different digests as equivocation: record a proposal-evidence pair, carry it into a block, and slash it like vote equivocation. Also stop relaying a second distinct-digest proposal from the same proposer (relay only the first per (height,round,proposer)).

findings.title: The overdraw ban is escaped when the banned payer also receives a same-block credit — the payer keeps its full balance and name, contradicting the documented/pinned 'balance destroyed' invariant
findings.description: ProcessPayments bans an overdrawing payer by skipping its outgoing (ledger.go:174) and excluding it from the pass-through loop (ledger.go:193). But the `affected` re-add loop (ledger.go:197-213) does NOT check `banned`: a banned payer that received ANY credit this block is in `affected`, so it is re-created from its ORIGINAL byKey balance plus the credit (its own debits were skipped), surviving with balance intact and its Name intact. findings.md's accepted design decision and TestOverdrawBanDestroysPayerBalance assert the account 'vanishes entirely'; that holds only when no same-block credit lands. Supply is still conserved (no mint), so this softens — not breaks — a safety property.
findings.failure_scenario: A holds 10, Name 'alice'. In one block A signs two 6-unit payments to B (12 > 10 → A banned) and C pays A 0.2. After ProcessPayments: A is re-added in the affected loop as 10 + 0.2 = 10.2 with Name 'alice' retained; B receives nothing; supply conserved. The documented harsh penalty (A destroyed) did not occur. This also means the hoarded-same-block-pair weaponization (findings.md second pass) can be dodged by any interleaving credit — benign direction, but it shows 'overdraw ⇒ balance destroyed' is not a reliable invariant and the regression test only covers the no-credit case.
findings.attacker: no attacker (inconsistency / safety-by-accident); relevant to the hoarded-pair weaponization recorded in findings.md
findings.known_status: new angle on the accepted overdraw-ban design decision (findings.md). The decision and TestOverdrawBanDestroysPayerBalance assume the balance is always destroyed; the same-block-credit escape is not covered — reporting it as the brief's explicit (e) question, not to reverse the accepted decision.
findings.poc: <scratch>/burn-rule/ledger/burnrule_poc_test.go — TestPoCOverdrawBanEscapedByIncomingCredit (FAIL: banned payer A present with 10.10 and name retained).
findings.fix: If the ban must mean 'destroyed', skip banned payers in the affected re-add loop too: `for k := range affected { if banned[k] { continue } ... }`. Otherwise document that an incoming same-block credit preserves a banned payer and relax the test accordingly.

findings.title: Docs claim slashing 'ejects the double-signer from the set' / 'zeroes it out' — the code removes an account, not the key's place in the validator set
findings.description: docs/managing-the-currency.md:40 says a double-signer 'is ejected from the set' (unconditional). docs/consensus.md:79 and README.md:77 say slashing 'removes the offender's account ... ejecting them from a dynamic set' and 'zeroes out the double-signer'. The code only deletes the account: in static mode the key stays in Config.Validators with full power (SLASH-1), and in dynamic mode delegated stake keeps it in the derived set (SLASH-2). So 'ejected from the set' is false in static mode and false in dynamic mode whenever others delegate to the offender. The design slogan 'two different signings means the key is burned' is likewise overstated: the account's balance is burned, the key is not.
findings.failure_scenario: An operator reads managing-the-currency.md and believes a caught double-signer is automatically removed from consensus, so no manual action is needed. In a static network (the documented default) the compromised validator keeps voting and, if ≥1/3, stalls the chain with no in-protocol recovery (SLASH-1). The operator has no doc warning that slashing is cosmetic for the consensus set in static mode, or that delegated stake defeats it in dynamic mode.
findings.attacker: no attacker (documentation)
findings.known_status: new. The brief requires flagging doc/README claims the code contradicts in this area.
findings.poc: none (documentation finding); the contradicted behavior is proven by SLASH-1 and SLASH-2 PoCs in <scratch>/burn-rule/node/burnrule_poc_test.go.
findings.fix: Either fix the code (SLASH-1/SLASH-2: a committed slashed-set removed from the effective validator set) and keep the docs, or correct the docs to state that slashing confiscates the account/stake but does NOT remove the key from a static Config.Validators set and is defeated by delegated stake in dynamic mode, with the manual re-genesis recovery step spelled out.

findings.title: Payments have no conflict/burn slot — the burn rule never fires against a leaked payment key (the owner's eMudhra hypothesis does not hold in this code)
findings.description: There is no equivocation concept for payments. Two different payments from one payer for the same BlockID are not flagged: either both apply (if the balance covers them) or the payer is overdraw-banned (ledger.go:160-181) — never recorded as a double-sign, never yielding durable evidence, never burning the key. admitPayment (node.go:432) refuses a second same-block payment only when it would overdraw; it is a refusal, not a burn. So the 'two different signings means the key is burned' principle simply does not cover the statement that moves money. A leaked/cracked key (the eMudhra scenario the owner cites) drains an account with ONE signing — there is no second conflicting signing for the rule to catch.
findings.failure_scenario: A thief obtains a user's key (leaked, or cracked from a low-entropy key as in eMudhra). The thief signs one payment draining the account for a near-future block the owner is not using. Honest intake accepts it (valid signature, funds present) and it commits. No 'two different signings' condition ever arises; the owner may never even produce a competing signature. The rule the owner expected to 'stop the issue immediately' is vote-only and does nothing here. Combined with NAME-1, the same leaked key also captures the victim's name. The rule protects consensus votes, not funds.
findings.attacker: holder of one stolen or cracked key
findings.known_status: new framing — directly answers the owner's stated hypothesis. The architecture is intentional (payments are authorised by one signature); the point is that the burn principle's scope excludes payments, so it provides no leaked-key protection.
findings.poc: none (architectural scope observation); the concrete end-state harm of a leaked key is demonstrated by NAME-1's PoCs (drain-to-zero + same-block name capture) in <scratch>/burn-rule/ledger/burnrule_poc_test.go.
findings.fix: Set expectations: the 'two signings = burn' rule is consensus-vote-only and cannot catch a single-signing drain. If leaked-key resilience for funds is wanted, add out-of-band mechanisms — key rotation/revocation, social recovery, or a hold/challenge window on large or name-changing transfers — rather than relying on equivocation detection.

findings.title: Account-update and governance-vote equivocation are undetected (two conflicting signings, no burn) — benign today, but the principle is absent
findings.description: Two conflicting AccountUpdates from one key for the same block both apply in order (account_update.go:83-114, last-wins, deterministic) — no conflict detected. A validator may sign parameter-vote (governance.go) and reassignment-vote (reassignment.go) approvals for multiple competing proposals at the same governance sequence; none is flagged as equivocation. These are benign: account-update last-wins is deterministic and same-key-only, and quorum intersection plus the single-use GovernanceSequence prevent two conflicting governance actions from both ratifying. But the burn principle is not applied here either. Separately, the declared domains validator-message (DomainValidatorMsg) and server-auth (DomainServerAuth) are UNUSED in the codebase (no Sign/Verify caller) — reserved slots, so no statement of those types exists to conflict.
findings.failure_scenario: No concrete harm. A validator double-votes YES on two contradictory reassignments at sequence N (e.g. grant Alice 1000 and grant Bob 1000); only one can enact because applying it bumps the sequence and the other becomes stale — no double-mint. A key signing two conflicting account-updates only changes its own attributes twice (last wins). Recorded for completeness of the matrix and because any future weakening of the quorum/sequence/determinism guards would turn these undetected equivocations into live risks.
findings.attacker: one validator (benign under current guards)
findings.known_status: new (matrix completeness). No prior finding covers non-vote equivocation detection; the dead domains are not noted in findings.md.
findings.poc: <scratch>/burn-rule/ledger/burnrule_poc_test.go — TestPoCConflictingAccountUpdatesBothApply (FAIL: both conflicting same-key updates applied, last wins, no detection).
findings.fix: Optional accountability only: detect and record conflicting same-key governance/account-update signings for the same slot if a social-punishment trail is wanted. Remove or document the unused validator-message/server-auth domains so they are not assumed to be protected statement types.

checked_ok: Vote (prevote/precommit) equivocation IS detected in-round and acted on: VoteSet.Add un-counts the second conflicting vote and records Evidence (consensus/voteset.go:160-169) — the one working link of the burn chain.

Equivocation evidence is unforgeable and cannot frame an honest key: Evidence.Valid requires both votes signed by the offender (consensus/evidence.go:11-22) and ApplyBlock rejects a block whose evidence does not verify (ledger/block.go:205-209); TestSlashRemovesEquivocator's framing case still passes.
Evidence is age-windowed (evidenceInWindow, maxEvidenceAge=1000, ledger/block.go:59-65) so stale evidence cannot be replayed against a recreated account — verified not regressed.

Quorum intersection (>⅔, consensus/validator.go:63) still prevents two conflicting block commits and two conflicting governance ratifications even if a validator double-votes across competing proposals.

Governance single-use via GovernanceSequence (ledger/parameters.go:319-323, bumped in ApplyBlock) prevents value-cycle replay of parameter/reassignment certificates — confirmed against TestChaosGovernanceCycleReplayStaysInert and reassignment_test.go.
Commit is round-scoped: Commit.Verify requires every precommit to share c.Round (consensus/commit.go:260), closing the mixed-round forge that would let a bad checkpoint verify.
Payment identity is content-based (PaymentID, ledger/payment.go:244), so a malleated signature cannot double-count a payment at mempool/gossip/ledger.
Gossip payment intake verifies the payer signature before admitting (node/httptransport.go:213), so the mempool cannot be filled with unsigned junk.
notes:
Burn-rule coverage matrix (signing/domain.go domains). 'Really burns the key?' = does a second conflicting signing permanently exclude the KEY?

| statement type (domain) | conflict slot | detected? | durable evidence? | penalty | really burns the key? |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| payment (DomainPayment) | same payer + same BlockID, different content | NO — not treated as equivocation | NO | either both apply, or overdraw-ban destroys the PAYER's balance (escapable, BAN-1) | NO — one signing drains; name hijackable (NAME-1); key recreatable, no tombstone |
| validator-message (DomainValidatorMsg) | none — domain DECLARED but UNUSED in code | n/a | n/a | none | n/a |
| account-update (DomainAccountUpdate) | same From + same BlockID, different content | NO | NO | none — both apply in order, last-wins (deterministic) | NO (benign, GOV-1) |
| server-auth (DomainServerAuth) | none — domain DECLARED but UNUSED in code | n/a | n/a | none | n/a |
| block-revision prevote/precommit (DomainBlockRevision) | same (height,round,type), different digest | YES — VoteSet.Add | YES — Evidence in Block.Evidence, age-windowed | applySlashes deletes offender's ACCOUNT | PARTIAL — account only; key stays in set (static: SLASH-1; dynamic via delegation: SLASH-2); account/name recreatable (NAME-1) |
| receipt (DomainReceipt) | none — a node may ack many payments; no exclusivity | NO | NO | none (a self-signed bogus receipt is evidence against the node, but no automated burn) | n/a |
| parameter-vote (DomainParameterVote) | validator signs two different changes at same sequence | NO | NO | none — quorum + single-use sequence prevent conflicting ratification | NO (benign, GOV-1) |
| reassignment-vote (DomainReassignmentVote) | validator signs two different reassignments at same sequence | NO | NO | none — as above | NO (benign, GOV-1) |
| proposal (DomainProposal) | proposer signs two proposals for same (height,round), different digest | NO — first-wins; Driver.Evidence scans only vote sets | NO | none; the second is even relayed + re-ApplyBlock'd network-wide (PROP-1) | NO |

Bottom line for the owner: the rule is live for exactly one row (block-revision votes), and even there it burns an account, not the key. It does not cover payments, so a leaked/cracked key is not burned by any 'two signings' rule — it is simply used to steal (PAY-1), and on the same block to seize the victim's name (NAME-1). The vindication the owner hoped for is not in the code as written.

summary: The consensus safety core is faithful Tendermint and held up under focused probing: quorum = floor(2·total/3)+1 with correct intersection, round-scoped Commit.Verify (distinct validators, tampered/mixed-round/below-quorum all rejected), a decision rule that fires only on a locally-held, ApplyBlock-validated, non-nil proposal plus a same-round precommit quorum (so a node cannot decide a value it never received or validated), POL verified against locally-received prevotes, the step≥prevote one-shot guard, the per-height validator set frozen at startHeight (so honest nodes agree), maxRoundLookahead bounding per-round allocation, and the checkpoint skipping-trust rule all check out — I found no fork/mint/fund-loss path under ≤1/3 Byzantine. The weaknesses are at the edges and mostly around the owner's own "two different signings = burned key" principle. (1) The vote intake is the one gossip path with no ingress verification, and the post-review vote-re-gossip machinery (an unbounded heightVotes map re-broadcast wholesale every tick) turns that into an amplifying, unbounded-memory DoS any port-reacher can trigger — a materially worse, newer surface than deferred #10. (2) Equivocation evidence is harvested only on the local-decide path, so a node that advances by catch-up silently drops it. (3) Proposal equivocation is entirely outside slashing. (4) Power saturation can invert the stake↔power premise at (assumed-away) >2^40 stakes.

findings.title: Unauthenticated vote intake + unbounded heightVotes + wholesale re-gossip = amplifying DoS
findings.description: handleVote decodes a Vote and calls SubmitVote with NO verification — unlike handlePay/handleGossipPayment/handleAccountUpdate, which VerifyPayment/VerifyAccountUpdate at ingress. In evVote the driver's ReceiveVote result is discarded, then rememberVote stores the vote keyed by validator+signature if v.Height==n.height (the ONLY thing checked — no signature, no validator-set membership, no round bound), and relay() re-broadcasts it. heightVotes has no cap (contrast mempool.maxSize). reGossipVotes then re-broadcasts the ENTIRE map to every peer each tick. So a non-validator who can POST /hdls/vote grows a node's memory without bound and makes every node flood the network with arbitrary junk every tick.
findings.failure_scenario: Attacker POSTs N distinct junk Vote JSONs (Height=current, junk Validator/Signature, absurd Round) to /hdls/vote. Each is stored in heightVotes (no cap) and relayed. Every reGossipVotes tick re-broadcasts all N to every peer, which store+relay+re-gossip them too — N×peers broadcasts network-wide per tick, unbounded N. PoC stored 5000 junk votes and re-broadcast all 5000 in one tick.
findings.attacker: anyone reaching the port (non-validator); worse with a stolen validator key, which also forces per-vote signature verification on every node each tick
findings.known_status: New angle on deferred #10 (unauthenticated write API / DoS). Materially worse: heightVotes is unbounded (no mempool-style cap) and the vote-re-gossip loop (a post-review liveness fix) amplifies one poster into a whole-network flood; the vote path is also the only gossip intake still lacking the ingress verification the gossip-payment fix added.
findings.poc: <scratch>/consensus-core/node/poc_consensus_core_test.go :: TestPoCUnverifiedVotesStoredUnboundedAndReGossiped (PASS — confirms 5000 unverified votes stored, 5000 re-broadcast in one tick)
findings.fix: Verify at vote ingress exactly like payments: check signature, validator-set membership, height, and round≤current+maxRoundLookahead BEFORE rememberVote/relay; store/re-gossip only accepted votes; cap heightVotes.

findings.title: Equivocation evidence is dropped when a node advances a height by catch-up instead of deciding locally
findings.description: A driver records equivocation (two conflicting votes for one height/round/type) as transferable Evidence. But the node harvests driver.Evidence() into pendingSlashes ONLY inside commit() (the local-decide path, node.go:644). A node that instead advances the height via catchUp() — verifyCheckpoint→fastForward→startHeight, the normal recovery when it fell behind — replaces the driver without harvesting, and fastForward does not touch pendingSlashes. So a double-signer the node witnessed during that height is never queued for slashing on that node. Also, late conflicting votes that arrive after commit() ran (same height, before the next startHeight) are added to the old driver but likewise never re-harvested. This weakens the owner's stated 'two different signings = burned key' guarantee.
findings.failure_scenario: Node is slightly behind. During height H it receives validator B's two conflicting prevotes (equivocation is detectable in its driver). Before it decides H locally, a peer's verified height-H checkpoint arrives; the node catches up to H+1. B's evidence, held only in the discarded H-driver, is never added to pendingSlashes — this node will never carry the slash. If every node that DID decide H locally also missed one of B's votes (loss/partition), B escapes the burn network-wide despite double-signing.
findings.attacker: one validator (the equivocator); exploited against nodes that resolve the height by catch-up
findings.known_status: New. The findings.md evidence items (#5 replay, maxEvidenceAge) concern re-including/aging evidence, not the harvest-skip on the catch-up path; this is a distinct lifetime gap. Safety (no fork) is unaffected — this is an accountability/deterrence gap.
findings.poc: <scratch>/consensus-core/node/poc_consensus_core_test.go :: TestPoCEquivocationEvidenceLostOnCatchUp (PASS — driver holds the evidence, pendingSlashes empty after catchUp to H+1)
findings.fix: Harvest driver.Evidence() into pendingSlashes in fastForward/catchUp as well as commit (evidence survives a height change regardless of how the height was resolved); consider retaining cross-height evidence for a bounded window.

findings.title: Proposal equivocation is unslashable and both conflicting proposals are relayed
findings.description: The owner's 'two signings = burned key' principle is enforced for VOTES (prevote/precommit → Evidence → slash) but not for PROPOSALS. The round's scheduled proposer can sign two different, validly-signed proposals for the same (height,round) — two signatures over conflicting statements by one key — and there is no evidence type or slash for it. Worse, onProposal relays BOTH: the held-proposal fast path (node.go:498) only dedups an IDENTICAL StateDigest, so a second, different-digest proposal from the same proposer passes the proposer+signature checks and returns true (relayed), flooding a second full block and splitting that round's prevote.
findings.failure_scenario: Byzantine proposer for (H, r) sends block A to half the nodes and block B to the other half, both validly signed. Each node relays whichever it sees first AND relays the other on arrival (fast path misses, different digest). The round's prevote splits; the round times out to nil. The proposer is never recorded as a double-signer. Over a height it can do this on every round it is selected for (~its stake fraction), a liveness tax plus doubled proposal bandwidth, at zero cost to its key.
findings.attacker: one validator (whichever is the round's scheduled proposer)
findings.known_status: New. Cannot fork (safety unaffected) and cannot stall permanently (honest-proposer rounds still commit); it is a bounded liveness/bandwidth tax plus a hole in the burned-key principle the owner cares about.
findings.poc: <scratch>/consensus-core/node/poc_consensus_core_test.go :: TestPoCProposerEquivocationUnslashedAndBothRelayed (PASS — both conflicting proposals accepted/relayed, no pendingSlashes entry)
findings.fix: Treat two differently-signed proposals for one (height,round) by the scheduled proposer as slashable proposal-equivocation evidence (a new Evidence variant over the proposal preimage); and never relay a second proposal for a round already held.

findings.title: Power saturation equalizes all above-cap validators, inverting the '<1/3 of stake' premise
findings.description: NewValidatorSet saturates any power >2^40 to exactly 2^40. The C2 decision framed this as keeping a whale's 'largest possible voice', but it also discards the true-stake ordering AMONG above-cap validators: a validator with true stake ~2^63 and one with true stake 2^40+1 end up with identical power. A by-count majority of above-cap validators then meets quorum regardless of how small their true-stake share is relative to a larger whale — breaking the stake==power premise behind docs/security.md's 'BFT up to <1/3 of stake'.
findings.failure_scenario: Set = {whale: true 2^63, byz1/byz2/byz3: true 2^40+1 each}. All four cap to 2^40. The three 'byz' (a vanishing fraction of the whale's true stake, i.e. far below 1/3 of true stake) hold 3·2^40 of capped power vs quorum ≈2.67·2^40 — they alone form a quorum and control finality. Governance/proposer views also show them as equals, masking the true disparity.
findings.attacker: <1/3 of true stake, but only reachable when multiple validators exceed 2^40 whole units — assumed away by the design, so no live break
findings.known_status: New angle on accepted C2 (truncation→saturation). C2 reasoned about the whale's own power not overflowing; it did not note that saturation equalizes multiple above-cap validators and can invert the BFT stake threshold. Also a docs-drift: security.md's '<1/3 of stake' claim does not hold once >1 validator exceeds the cap.
findings.poc: <scratch>/consensus-core/node/poc_consensus_core_test.go :: TestPoCSaturationEqualizesAboveCapValidators (PASS)
findings.fix: If saturation can ever trigger in a deployment, scale all powers down by a common factor to preserve ratios instead of clamping independently; otherwise document that the <1/3-of-stake guarantee assumes no validator exceeds 2^40 whole units.

checked_ok: Commit.Verify is round-scoped and rejects mixed-round, wrong-Round, duplicate-voter, tampered, and below-quorum certificates (consensus/commit.go:155-172; consensus_test TestCommitRejectsMixedRounds et al.) — the forged-certificate-on-onboarding HIGH stays fixed.

Decision rule (driver.go:303-312) fires only on a locally-held proposal that is p.Valid (ApplyBlock-validated by the caller), non-nil, with a same-round precommit quorum — a node cannot decide a value it never received or never validated, and never decides nil.

Proof-of-lock is verified against the node's OWN prevote set (driver.go:337-340 checks d.prevotes[vr].HasQuorumFor), not trusted from the proposal; the unlock/lock rules (prevoteFor, driver.go:385-398) match Tendermint and the POL-release and conflicting-prevote tests pass.
The step>=StepPrevote guard on the 2/3-prevote one-shot (driver.go:349) is present, preventing the propose-step consumption stall.

maxRoundLookahead (256) bounds per-round VoteSet allocation; negative and far-future rounds are rejected before ensureRound (driver.go:216-218); future-HEIGHT votes are dropped by the driver (not buffered).

Per-height validator set is frozen once at startHeight (node.go:472) and reused by driver, onProposal, and commit — in dynamic mode all honest nodes derive the same set from identical committed state, so they cannot disagree on who verifies votes for height H.

Checkpoint skipping-trust rule is sound: Commit.Verify against the carried signing set + digest-binding to the supplied accounts + >1/3 anchor-power overlap (node.go:388-401); a fabricated all-stranger set has no anchor overlap and a nil-digest commit cannot bind a real SHA-256 state digest.

Proposer selection (validator.go ProposerAt) is a deterministic pure function of (height,round,set) via FNV, returns '' for an empty/zero-power set, and is stake-weighted without a usable single-key grind (seed is fixed by height/round).
Equivocation Evidence.Valid is unforgeable (both votes must carry the offender's own signatures), so an honest validator cannot be framed; in-round un-counting of equivocators is correct.

onProposal authenticates proposals against driver.Proposer(round) and VerifyProposal before use, and does not relay an identical-digest duplicate — the unauthenticated-front-run HIGH stays fixed (the residual is the different-digest relay in SLASH-2).
notes: On the owner's "two different signings = burned key" principle: it is correctly and robustly enforced for the safety-critical case — a validator that signs two conflicting PREVOTES or PRECOMMITS for the same (height,round) is caught as unforgeable Evidence, un-counted in-round, and slashed out of state, and this cannot fork the chain. The gaps this review surfaced are at the principle's edges, not its core: (a) evidence is harvested only on the local-decide path, so a node that advances by catch-up drops it (SLASH-1); and (b) a double-signed PROPOSAL (also two signings over conflicting statements by one key) is entirely outside the evidence/slash machinery (SLASH-2). Neither breaks no-fork safety, but both mean a key that "signs two different things" is not always burned, contrary to the stated design intent — worth closing if that principle is to be relied on after a key-compromise event.

area: ledger-transition (ledger/*.go state transition: ProcessPayments, ProposeBlock/ApplyBlock, digest, account updates, payments, parameters/topology as they feed the digest)
summary: The arithmetic and conservation core is sound for well-formed input, and propose/apply symmetry holds for accepted blocks: both paths run the same payments → updates → slashes → reassignment pipeline under the pre-block parameters, and ApplyBlock rejects wherever ProposeBlock filters. The digest covers every Account field, every parameter and the governance sequence. The governance-sequence replay fixes hold. The weak points are at the boundaries. (1) Nothing bounds a block, so fee-free updates can make every proposal undeliverable and halt the chain (PoC). (2) Amounts are decoded and size-checked too late: exponent-form big.Rat fields cost about 1.5 MB each at decode, and balances can grow without bound past the per-message cap. (3) Identity is a string, not a key, and a name is tied to the balance lifecycle: base64 aliases, and names released at zero balance and claimable in the same block. (4) Relative to the owner's 'two different signings means the key is burned' principle, a slash removes only the offender's own account. Delegated stake keeps the key in the dynamic set, the static set is untouched, and nothing tombstones the key. The overdraw ban, meanwhile, fires on a single over-balance payment, which the documented wallet closure does not cover. Each finding is backed by a failing PoC in the scratch copy except TOPO-1 (low confidence, script-only evidence).

findings.title: No per-block size bound: fee-free updates push every proposal past peers' 1 MiB decode limit and halt the chain
findings.description: MaxMessageBytes bounds each message, but nothing bounds a block. ProposeBlock carries every valid payment and update naming the height, and ApplyBlock accepts any number of them. Every receiver, though, decodes a proposal under a 1 MiB body limit. Account updates carry no fee, and the update pool admits any BlockID. So pooled content for one height can push every honest proposer's candidate (built once per height from the whole gossiped pools) past 1 MiB. Peers fail to decode it and prevote nil. The next proposer's candidate fails the same way, and nothing evicts the content, because pools are pruned only on commit.
findings.failure_scenario: PoC on a 4-validator HTTP network: one account holding 1 unit signs 600 distinct updates, each 2000 bytes or less (within the default cap), all naming height 3, and they are gossiped to all nodes. Heights 1-2 commit. The candidate for height 3 serializes to 1,159,040 bytes, and the chain stays at height 3 for 100 s with all validators up (heights=[3 3 3 3]). A control run with 400 updates (772,841 bytes) commits in 1.2 s. Below-cost payments (FEE-1) are a second fee-free way to fill a block.
findings.attacker: any account holder (no fee; a 1-unit balance suffices)
findings.known_status: new. The findings.md third pass added a per-message bound only; there is no per-block bound. Distinct from deferred #10 (request flooding).
findings.poc: <scratch>/ledger-transition/node/poc_oversize_block_test.go: TestPoCOversizeBlockStallsHeight FAILs (stalled at height 3); control TestPoCOversizeBlockControlUnderLimit PASSes. Run with GOLEDGER_CHAOS_SLACK=4.
findings.fix: Add a governed per-block byte budget (well under the transport limit) plus a count cap. ProposeBlock fills deterministically up to it, and ApplyBlock rejects blocks over it. Charge a fee for account updates or cap them per account per block. Refuse BlockIDs beyond height+window at intake, and drop pooled content for a height after N failed rounds.

findings.title: Exponent-form big.Rat amounts: an 11-byte JSON field costs ~1.5 MB of heap and seconds of CPU before any size check
findings.failure_scenario: Measured: decoding 40 fields of {"Amount":"1p9999999"} (921 bytes) adds 59 MB of live heap, 1529 KB per field. A 1 MiB body holds about 45k such fields, roughly 66 GB extrapolated (not run on the shared machine). Any POST to /hdls/proposal, /hdls/pay or /hdls/payment is decoded this way before authentication. A validly signed payment carrying that amount costs 1.42 s in VerifyPayment and 1.55 s in WithinMessageBound per submission before it is refused.
findings.attacker: anyone reaching the port
findings.known_status: Related to deferred #10 (unauthenticated API / rate limiting). New angle: a single small request amplifies 10^4-10^5x in memory and CPU, which per-client rate limiting does not bound.
findings.poc: <scratch>/ledger-transition/ledger/poc_rat_decode_amplification_test.go: TestPoCRatDecodeAmplification FAILs (1529 KB of heap per 22-byte field; VerifyPayment 1.42 s, WithinMessageBound 1.55 s).
findings.fix: Give amounts a custom JSON type that accepts only plain "a/b" or decimal strings with a digit cap and no exponent, before allocating. Add a cheap Num().BitLen()+Denom().BitLen() precheck in WithinMessageBound and before any RatString (VerifyPayment, PaymentID, intake). Bound the checkpoint response body, and require Content-Type: application/json.

findings.title: A slash does not burn the key: delegated stake keeps the equivocator in the dynamic set, the static set is untouched, and there is no tombstone
findings.description: applySlashes removes only the account whose PublicKey is the offender's. In this DPoS design most of a validator's power is delegated, i.e. comes from accounts whose ValidatorNode points at it. Those accounts are untouched, and deriveValidators keeps summing them, so the equivocator stays a validator with nearly unchanged power. In static mode the slash never affects the configured set. Nothing records the key as burned, so it can be re-funded or re-delegated and keeps voting, proposing and signing governance votes. The node re-carries the evidence every block until the 1000-block window closes, because the offender is still 'a validator'. README, consensus.md and managing-the-currency.md all claim the slash ejects the offender from the set.
findings.failure_scenario: PoC: dynamic threshold 100; validator V owns 10, and two delegators delegate 400 each to V. A block with valid equivocation evidence against V applies and V's own account is removed. deriveValidators still reports V as a validator with power 800 (it was 810). A leaked validator key that is caught double-signing therefore keeps its voting power.
findings.attacker: one validator (an equivocating or leaked validator key)
findings.known_status: new. The findings.md MEDIUM (evidence replay against recreated accounts) was fixed with an age window; nothing addresses delegated stake or exclusion of the key. Contradicts the owner's burned-key principle and the README/docs claims (docs-drift).
findings.poc: <scratch>/ledger-transition/node/poc_slash_delegation_test.go: TestPoCSlashDoesNotEjectDelegatedValidator FAILs (power 810 → 800, still a validator).
findings.fix: Add a committed BurnedKeys set to LedgerState, bound into the digest; valid evidence adds the key. deriveValidators and the node's static set exclude burned keys regardless of delegations, and votes, proposals and governance votes from burned keys are refused. Optionally reset delegations that point at a burned key back to their owners.

findings.title: Zero-balance deletion releases a registered name; another account can claim it in the same block and receive pay-by-name payments
findings.description: An account whose balance reaches zero is deleted, and its Name goes with it, with no owner-signed release. applyAccountUpdates runs after payments, against the post-payment accounts, so a fee-free update from any other account naming that block claims the freed name in the same block. Pay-by-name payments resolve at apply time. Payments already signed by name for later blocks, and all future ones, therefore credit the new holder. The user manual's migration advice ('create a fresh wallet there and pay yourself to it') empties the old account, and bans and slashes release names the same way. No doc says that emptying an account gives up its name.
findings.failure_scenario: PoC: Alice ('alice', balance 10) moves 10 to her new wallet in block 5, and the same block carries another account's update claiming 'alice'. Bob's payment of 20 to 'alice', signed earlier for block 6, credits the claimant (1 → 20.90). The claimant keeps the name (first-come), so later payers typing 'alice' also pay it.
findings.attacker: any account holder (fee-free update), once the name holder's balance reaches zero or it is banned or slashed
findings.known_status: new. The findings.md third pass moved name resolution on-chain; the release-on-zero lifecycle is not discussed anywhere.
findings.poc: <scratch>/ledger-transition/ledger/poc_name_release_test.go: TestPoCZeroBalanceReleasesNameToAnotherKey FAILs (the claimant owns 'alice' and is credited with Bob's payment).
findings.fix: Decouple identity from balance. Keep accounts that hold a Name, delegation or Address at zero balance, or tombstone a released name for a governed grace period. Release a name only through an owner-signed update. Warn in the wallet and manual.

findings.title: Overdraw ban fires on a single over-balance payment; the wallet signs any amount, so the documented same-block closure does not protect honest payers
findings.description: The ban (an accepted design) destroys the payer's whole balance whenever its outgoing in a block exceeds its balance. One payment is enough, as is a later-block payment that exceeds what an earlier one left. The second-pass closure assumes the trigger needs two same-block payments, and stops only that case. The wallet has no local balance check: it signs whatever amount is typed and posts it, and only then gets the node's 409. Honest proposers never include such a payment, but a block that does is fully valid. Docs-drift: the manual says a refused payment means 'nothing is debited', and security.md says an honest user cannot trip the ban.
findings.failure_scenario: PoC: a payer holds 10 and signs one payment of 100. A block carrying it at its BlockID applies, and the payer's account (10) is destroyed. In practice: a typo of 100 instead of 10 is refused with 409 by the reference node, which now holds the signature. If that validator is the proposer at the payment's BlockID and includes it, the payer's whole balance is destroyed. The wallet derives the BlockID from the height that same node reports.
findings.attacker: one validator acting as the payer's reference node (proposer at the payment's BlockID)
findings.known_status: Relates to the accepted overdraw-ban DESIGN DECISION and its second-pass wallet closure. New angle: the closure is incomplete, because a single payment with no same-block pair triggers the ban. security.md, USER_MANUAL.md and the wallet.go comment overstate the protection.
findings.poc: <scratch>/ledger-transition/ledger/poc_overdraw_semantics_test.go: TestPoCOverdrawBanSemantics FAILs (case 1: a block with one over-balance payment applies and the payer is destroyed).
findings.fix: Ledger: drop a lone over-balance payment without destroying the balance, and reserve the ban for provable double-spends (two or more distinct same-block payments, each individually within the balance). Wallet: track balance minus pending locally and refuse to sign more. Correct the docs.

findings.title: Below-cost payments are admitted, receipted and carried by honest nodes with no fee; other zero-fee no-ops still pass ApplyBlock
findings.description: ProcessPayments silently drops payments that are below the cost, come from a non-existent payer, or duplicate another payment's content: no debit, no fee. The release-candidate fix kept only unresolvable-recipient payments out of blocks. Honest intake rejects only non-positive amounts, so a below-cost payment gets a receipt, is gossiped, and is carried by honest proposers for free. Intake has no upper bound on BlockID, and the overdraw guard just sums amounts. So tiny payments naming a far-future block can sit in the bounded mempool indefinitely and get honest payments refused. Proposers can also pad blocks with phantom-payer or duplicate payments and with no-op updates.
findings.failure_scenario:
PoCs:
- 50 of 50 payments of 0.001 (fee 0.1) are admitted, all 50 are carried in the honest proposal, the block applies, and the payer is charged nothing.
- With a 50-slot pool, 50 such payments naming block 2^40 survive dropBelow while locking 5e-8 units, and an honest 5-unit payment is refused ('mempool full').
- A block carrying a ghost-payer payment, a below-cost payment and a ghost update applies with no state change.
findings.attacker: any account holder (tiny balance)
findings.known_status: Partially fixed: the RC review closed unresolvable recipients only, and the original findings.md gossip-intake HIGH noted far-future residency (its signature fix stands). New: below-cost amounts remove the overdraw guard's economic bound.
findings.poc: <scratch>/ledger-transition/node/poc_below_cost_intake_test.go: TestPoCBelowCostPaymentAdmittedAndCarriedFree and TestPoCBelowCostFarFutureFillsMempool both FAIL. <scratch>/ledger-transition/ledger/poc_noop_and_pin_test.go: TestPoCApplyBlockAcceptsOtherZeroFeeNoOps FAILs.
findings.fix: Refuse Amount < cost at intake. ProposeBlock should filter, and ApplyBlock reject, every payment ProcessPayments would drop (below cost, absent payer, duplicate content) and every no-op update (absent account). Bound BlockID to height+window at intake.

findings.title: State digest encodes nil and zero amounts identically; a checkpoint with null amounts verifies and then panics the state transition
findings.description: StateDigest writes "0" for a nil Amount, the same bytes as a real zero, so two different account sets share one committed digest. Zero-balance accounts are reachable in committed state: a ⅔ reassignment to 0 keeps the account, and genesis may contain "0". A peer serving a checkpoint can replace such an amount with null. verifyCheckpoint checks only the commit and the digest, so the node adopts it. The next block that credits or debits that account dereferences nil in ProcessPayments and panics. The run loop has no recover, so the process exits, and the snapshot it already wrote holds the null, so restarts fail the same way.
findings.failure_scenario: PoC: a ratified reassignment sets 'coop' to 0. The committed state and a copy with coop's Amount=nil have equal LedgerState digests, and node-level verifyCheckpoint accepts the null-amount checkpoint. Applying the next honest block (a payment to 'coop') on the adopted state panics with a nil pointer dereference.
findings.attacker: a gossip or bootstrap peer serving /hdls/checkpoint (catch-up sources default to gossip peers)
findings.known_status: new
findings.poc: <scratch>/ledger-transition/ledger/poc_digest_nil_amount_test.go: TestPoCDigestConflatesNilAndZeroAmount FAILs (same digest, then a panic). <scratch>/ledger-transition/node/poc_checkpoint_nil_amount_test.go: TestPoCCheckpointWithNilAmountVerifies FAILs.
findings.fix: Make the digest injective (encode nil distinctly, or reject nil amounts). Validate adopted checkpoints and snapshots before fastForward: non-nil and non-negative amounts, canonical and unique keys, unique names. Treat nil as zero defensively in ProcessPayments, and consider a recover-and-halt in the run loop.

findings.title: One Ed25519 key has unboundedly many accepted base64 spellings; in dynamic mode it can hold several validator identities and equivocate across them without evidence
findings.description: Identities are compared as strings, but signatures verify against the decoded key. Go's base64 decoding ignores the 2 trailing bits of a 32-byte key and any \r or \n, even with Strict(). So one key has 4 spellings, plus unboundedly many with embedded newlines. Stake delegated under two spellings creates two validator identities for one key. That key can cast one conflicting vote per spelling in the same (height, round, type): both are counted, the VoteSet records no equivocation, and Evidence.Valid rejects a cross-spelling pair. 'Two different signings means the key is burned' is enforced per spelling, not per key. Payments to an alias also create a separate account for the same key.
findings.failure_scenario: PoC: D1 delegates 400 to V's canonical string and D2 delegates 400 to an alias. deriveValidators yields both identities (400 + 400 of 1700). V signs prevote X as V and prevote Y as the alias at height 9, round 0. Both are counted, no evidence is recorded, and hand-built evidence is invalid.
findings.attacker: one validator (controls the delegation strings of its own accounts)
findings.known_status: new
findings.poc: <scratch>/ledger-transition/node/poc_key_alias_test.go: TestPoCKeyAliasEvadesEquivocationDetection FAILs.
findings.fix: Accept a key string only if it decodes to 32 bytes and base64.StdEncoding.EncodeToString(decoded) == s. Enforce this in signing.VerifyBase64 and wherever the ledger stores a key (PublicKeyTo, Delegated, genesis, Validator fields), rejecting non-canonical keys at intake and in ApplyBlock. Strict() alone is not enough.

findings.title: MaxMessageBytes bounds messages, not balances: coprime-denominator payments grow one balance without limit, at super-linear digest and arithmetic cost
findings.description: Each in-bound payment can carry an amount whose denominator is coprime to the balance's. The balance's denominator becomes their LCM, growing by roughly the per-message digit budget per payment. Every LedgerState.Digest RatString-encodes every balance, several times per block per node, and Cmp/Add/Sub on such balances pay big-number multiply and GCD costs. The owner cannot normalize the balance, because an amount with that denominator exceeds the cap. Once the encoding passes 1 MiB, no reassignment can carry the exact PreviousAmount either. Cost is one fee per payment: free if transactionCost is 0 (documented as allowed), and a single payment suffices if MaxMessageBytes is 0.
findings.failure_scenario: PoC (shared machine, so timings are approximate): 1000 payments of 0.1+1/d_i, each within the 2000-byte cap, cost 100 units of fees. Afterwards the payee's and payer's balances each encode to about 1.56 MB. StateDigest takes about 0.9 s per call, and one ordinary 1-unit payment touching these accounts takes about 13.5 s in ProcessPayments, beyond typical step timeouts, on every node.
findings.attacker: any account holder paying fees (free if transactionCost is 0)
findings.known_status: Relates to the findings.md third-pass item 'one fee could buy an arbitrarily large permanent ledger entry — FIXED'. That fix bounds messages, not accumulated balances.
findings.poc: <scratch>/ledger-transition/ledger/poc_rat_growth_test.go: TestPoCBalanceRepresentationGrowsPastMessageCap FAILs (1,560,790-byte balance; digest about 0.9 s; one payment 13.5 s; runs about 90 s).
findings.fix: Fix the money unit: require amounts and the cost to be integer multiples of a governed smallest unit (e.g. 10^-8), so every denominator divides a fixed D and every balance's size is bounded. Alternatively, reject any payment whose application would push a balance's encoding over a bound.

findings.title: A banned payer that also receives a credit in the same block keeps its whole balance
findings.description: The design decision says a banned payer is 'dropped from the result entirely'. In the code, a banned payer is skipped only in the pass-through loop. If any payment in the block credits it, by key or via a name it holds, it lands in `affected` and is re-added with its old balance plus the credit; its own payments are merely skipped. Whether the ban destroys anything therefore depends on unrelated payments the proposer chooses to include. TestOverdrawBanDestroysPayerBalance does not cover this case.
findings.failure_scenario: PoC: A (balance 10) sends two 6-unit payments, which bans it, and C pays A 1 in the same block. A remains with 10.90 instead of being destroyed.
findings.attacker: no attacker (semantics); the proposer decides by including or omitting a credit
findings.known_status: Relates to the accepted overdraw-ban DESIGN DECISION. New: the documented trace is incomplete.
findings.poc: <scratch>/ledger-transition/ledger/poc_overdraw_semantics_test.go: TestPoCOverdrawBanSemantics FAILs (case 2: A present with 10.90).
findings.fix: Decide which behaviour is intended and pin it with a regression test. Either skip banned keys in the affected loop too, or document that a same-block credit preserves the account.

findings.title: PrevStateDigest tier compares the account-only digest, but the docs and the API point clients at the full committed digest
findings.description: The Payment field comment says a pinned payment is included only in a block whose PrevStateDigest matches, and the operator guide says 'prior state'. Block.PrevStateDigest is the full LedgerState digest (accounts + parameters + sequence), and it is what /hdls/resolve reports as stateDigest. The ledger, however, compares the pin against StateDigest(accounts) only. A client following the docs builds a payment that can never be included. admitPayment doesn't check the field, so the client still gets a receipt. Pinning only the account digest also leaves parameter and governance history unpinned.
findings.failure_scenario: PoC: a payment pinned to hex(prev.Digest()), which equals the block's PrevStateDigest, is excluded by ProposeBlock.
findings.attacker: no attacker (bug)
findings.known_status: new
findings.poc: <scratch>/ledger-transition/ledger/poc_noop_and_pin_test.go: TestPoCPrevStateDigestPinPerDocsNeverIncludable FAILs.
findings.fix: In both paths, compare the pin against previousState.Digest() (the block's PrevStateDigest). Alternatively, expose the account digest and correct the docs. Check the pin at intake.

findings.title: Genesis accepts duplicate keys, zero or negative amounts and duplicate names; a duplicated key silently loses balance
findings.description: load() validates genesis amounts only for parse errors. ProcessPayments collapses a duplicated key through its map (the last entry wins) the first time the key is touched, destroying the other entry's balance. A negative genesis balance increases the supply sum when its holder is banned, and duplicate names resolve last-wins. StateDigest's comment says the digest must not depend on input order, but SliceStable makes it depend on the order of duplicates. One config typo makes states reachable that the transition itself never produces; all nodes share the config, so there is no fork.
findings.failure_scenario: PoC: genesis A:10, A:5, B:1; A pays B 1. Supply goes from 16 to 5.90, i.e. 10 units are lost beyond the 0.1 fee. Swapping the duplicate entries changes the digest.
findings.attacker: no attacker (operator typo)
findings.known_status: new
findings.poc: <scratch>/ledger-transition/ledger/poc_genesis_duplicates_test.go: TestPoCGenesisDuplicateKeyBreaksConservation FAILs.
findings.fix: Validate genesis in load(): unique canonical 32-byte keys, positive amounts, and unique names no longer than MaxAccountNameLength. Fix the digest comment.

findings.title: Consensus-critical Acceptable() depends on float Pow/Ceil at integer boundaries
findings.description: GroupParameters derives the gossip dimension with math.Ceil(math.Pow(n, 1/e)). That dimension decides TimingConsistent → Acceptable → ParameterChange.Valid inside ApplyBlock. math.Pow is not correctly rounded and is not bit-identical across Go ports: amd64 uses assembly Exp/Log, other ports use pure Go. At perfect powers the result can land just above or below the integer: on amd64, 125^(1/3) = 5.0000000000000009, so Ceil gives 6. Comparing amd64 with GOARCH=386, 5 of 141 perfect powers differ bit-wise, but none of those differences straddle an integer.
findings.failure_scenario: Hypothetical: validators on two architectures compute different dimensions for the same (participants, maxPeers). A ⅔-ratified profile whose StepTimeoutMs sits between the two thresholds is then valid on one side and invalid on the other, and the block carrying it splits the validators.
findings.attacker: no attacker (bug)
findings.known_status: new
findings.poc: none: the only evidence is a standalone script comparing math.Pow bits on amd64 and 386 (5 of 141 differ); no divergence that crosses an integer was demonstrated.
findings.fix: Compute the group size and dimension with integer arithmetic (an integer k-th root by binary search).

checked_ok: Propose/apply symmetry for accepted blocks: both run ProcessPayments → applyAccountUpdates → applySlashes → applyReassignment under the pre-block TransactionCost and MaxMessageBytes, and ApplyBlock rejects wherever ProposeBlock filters (signature, BlockID, pin, size, recipient, evidence window, governance validity, at most one governance action).

Digest coverage: all six Account fields (incl. Address), all five LedgerParameters fields and GovernanceSequence are hashed; sub-digests are fixed-size; fields are length-prefixed; JSON-decoded Rats are normalized, so RatString is canonical (the only collision is DIGEST-1's nil vs 0).
Governance replay: ParameterChange and Reassignment are bound to the sequence and single-use in both paths; at most one governance action per block is enforced.
No mint through payments: negative or nil cost is clamped, negative amounts are excluded, phantom payers can't mint, malleated copies dedup by PaymentID, and self-payment nets exactly -fee.

Pay-by-name resolves against the pre-block registry in ProcessPayments and in both block filters, so a same-block name move cannot fork resolution; payments naming both or neither recipient are rejected in both paths and at intake.
Copy-on-write: ProcessPayments allocates fresh Rats, and applyAccountUpdates/applyReassignment copy the slice, so the previous state is never mutated.
Multiple updates for one key or one name in a block apply deterministically in block order; the first claimant in block order wins a contested free name.
Evidence verification (same validator string, same h/r/type, different digests, both signatures valid) and the evidence age window are enforced in both paths.
MaxAccountNameLength (32) keeps names distinct from canonical 44-character keys.
notes:
