Status of the 'two different signings means the key is burned' principle in this ledger:

| Signing | Detected as a burn signal? | What actually happens |
|---|---|---|
| Two conflicting consensus votes, same Validator string, same h/r/type | Yes (Evidence) | Only the offender's own account is removed. Delegations keep it in the dynamic set, the static set is unchanged, and the key can be re-funded (SLASH-1). |
| The same key under two spellings | No | Conflicting votes evade detection (KEYALIAS-1). |
| Conflicting proposals, conflicting governance votes for one sequence, receipts | No | Never turned into evidence (outside the ledger area; flag for the consensus and governance reviewers). |
| Payments | Overdraw ban is the only analog | Fires on a single over-balance payment (OVERDRAW-1) and is undone by any same-block credit (OVERDRAW-2). |

Caveats:
- RAT-DECODE-1's 1 MiB figure is extrapolated linearly from a 40-field decode (59 MB). I deliberately did not run the full body on the shared machine.
- RAT-GROWTH-1's timings were taken on a shared, loaded machine. That test takes about 90 s; BLOCK-SIZE-1 takes about 100 s with GOLEDGER_CHAOS_SLACK=4.
- Minor hygiene (not reported as a finding): evidenceInWindow computes height - e.A.Height without overflow care, so votes signed at heights near MinInt64 stay 'in window' forever. Only the offender's own key can produce them, which is harmless and consistent with burning.

Re-run all PoCs:
cd <scratch>/ledger-transition && go test -count=1 -run TestPoC -v ./ledger/ && GOLEDGER_CHAOS_SLACK=4 go test -count=1 -short -run TestPoC -v ./node/

The original tree was not modified. The baseline ledger and node suites pass in the scratch copy with the PoCs skipped, and go vet is clean.

summary: The ⅔ certificate machinery (sequence single-use guard, quorum math, duplicate/unknown-voter rejection, non-negative guard, at-most-one-action-per-block, full-profile digest coverage) is sound WITHIN a single live chain. The weaknesses are at the seams. Two break supply/liveness invariants the docs advertise as guaranteed: a reassignment is validated against the pre-block balance but applied as an ABSOLUTE set AFTER payments, so an account's same-block outflow is minted a second time (unratified inflation, invisible per-account); and LedgerParameters.Acceptable has only lower timing bounds, so a ⅔ vote can set a block interval of centuries and halt the chain irreversibly. Two more are unauthenticated-reach problems into the governance pools (permanent freeze by slot-squatting; a ~500-byte packet stalling the event loop ~9s via big.Rat exponent amplification). The eMudhra "burned key" principle does not hold here: in no validator mode does slashing durably remove a proven double-signer's voting/governance power. Plus a pooled-vote poisoning liveness wedge and a cross-re-genesis certificate/payment replay. All seven are traced end-to-end with failing PoCs.

findings.title: Reassignment applied post-payments as an absolute set mints the target's same-block outflow
findings.description: Reassignment.Valid checks the account holds PreviousAmount in the PRE-block state (reassignment.go:90), but ApplyBlock runs ProcessPayments first and applyReassignment last (block.go:230-234), setting the balance to the ABSOLUTE NewAmount. If the target's key-holder sends an outgoing payment naming the enacting block, the outflow is honoured (payee credited) AND the balance is re-set to NewAmount regardless — so whatever was moved out is created from nothing. Supply grows by (moved-out amount) beyond the ratified delta. An honest proposer builds this block: ProposeBlock carries both; ApplyBlock accepts it. The docs note the INBOUND direction (a same-block credit is overwritten) but not that the OUTBOUND direction mints. Breaks the B1/B2 'supply integrity, fixed by construction' claim via governance, and the 'every mint == its certificate' auditability managing-the-currency.md relies on (the extra mint is laundered as an ordinary payment).
findings.failure_scenario: Treasury custodian holds key T (balance 1000), NOT a validator. The ⅔ set ratifies a treasury top-up 1000→5000. Custodian signs a payment T→X(own 2nd key) of 1000 naming block h; honest intake admits it (pending 1000 ≤ balance 1000). The proposer of h carries both. ApplyBlock: ProcessPayments debits T, credits X 999.9; applyReassignment sets T=5000. Result: T=5000, X=999.9 — supply +4999.9 while the certificate ratified +4000. 999.9 minted per top-up, repeatable. A ⅔ seizure 1000→0 is likewise defeated: victim pre-signs an outflow into the seizure block, keeps the money at X, account zeroes — confiscation nets nothing.
findings.attacker: holder of one key that is the subject of any ⅔-ratified reassignment (e.g. a treasury custodian; or a seizure target)
findings.known_status: Related to findings.md LOW 'Reassignment validated pre-block but applied post-payments', which only documents the INBOUND case (a same-block credit silently overwritten, no supply effect). This is the OUTBOUND case: materially worse — it MINTS supply and defeats ⅔ seizures. New angle, not recorded.
findings.poc: <scratch>/governance/ledger/zz_govreview_poc_test.go (TestPoCGovReassignmentSameBlockOutflowIsMintedTwice) — FAILs: top-up and both seizure sizes each mint 999.9
findings.fix: Validate and apply the reassignment against POST-payment balances (move the PreviousAmount check into ApplyBlock after ProcessPayments), or forbid a block that carries a reassignment for an account that also appears as a payer/payee that block, or apply it as a delta (NewAmount-PreviousAmount) rather than an absolute set.

findings.title: LedgerParameters.Acceptable has no upper timing bound: a ⅔ vote can halt the chain irreversibly
findings.description: Acceptable/TimingConsistent (parameters.go:76-97) enforce only LOWER bounds: StepTimeoutMs>0, BlockIntervalMs>=0, MaxPeers>=0, StepTimeoutMs >= dimension*250. There is no CEILING on BlockIntervalMs or StepTimeoutMs. A ⅔-ratified ParameterChange can set BlockIntervalMs to billions of ms (centuries). After the enacting block commits, node.commit schedules evNextHeight that far in the future (node.go:671-678 via blockInterval), so the chain produces no further block. Because every governance action (including a revert) needs a block, nothing on-chain can undo it — the network is bricked until a manual re-genesis. MinMessageBytes exists precisely so governance cannot vote a chain-bricking value; the timing fields have no equivalent guard, despite the wallet/docs treating Acceptable as the brick-proofing. (StepTimeoutMs=MaxInt64 instead overflows time.Duration to negative, causing immediate-timeout round churn.)
findings.failure_scenario: Validators holding ⅔ (or one validator in a small set) vote a profile with BlockIntervalMs=86_400_000_000 ('one day' mistyped with extra zeros, ~2.7 years) and otherwise-current fields. It passes Valid (Acceptable=true) and enacts. The enacting block commits; the next height is scheduled ~2.7 years out. The validator immediately votes the revert — it pools but is never carried into a block, because no block is ever produced. Chain halted permanently; only an out-of-band coordinated re-genesis recovers it. A hostile ⅔ coalition can do this deliberately as a kill switch; an honest fat-finger does it by accident.
findings.attacker: a ⅔ validator coalition, or any single validator in a set whose quorum it meets (e.g. a one-validator or skewed-power deployment)
findings.known_status: New. TODO.md 'More governable parameters' notes 'extend Acceptable if it has an invariant' and the MinMessageBytes floor is the precedent for brick-proofing — the timing fields were given a lower bound but no upper bound. Not in findings.md.
findings.poc: ledger: .../governance/ledger/zz_govreview_poc_test.go (TestPoCGovAcceptableAllowsChainHaltingTiming) — FAILs, Valid=true for 2.7-yr and 285-yr intervals and MaxInt64 step. node: .../governance/node/zz_govreview_poc_test.go (TestPoCGovHugeBlockIntervalHaltsChain) — FAILs: live node stops committing, revert never enacts
findings.fix: Add sane upper bounds to Acceptable (e.g. BlockIntervalMs and StepTimeoutMs each <= a few minutes/hours max), mirroring the MinMessageBytes floor, so a ratified profile can never stop block production. Also clamp StepTimeoutMs to avoid the Duration overflow.

findings.title: Governance vote pools are fillable with unauthenticated voteless entries, freezing governance permanently
findings.description: addParameterVotes/addReassignmentVotes allocate a pool slot for a proposal BEFORE verifying any vote (governance.go:47-54, reassignment.go:49-54): a ParameterChange with an Acceptable profile and ZERO (or bogus-signature) votes still creates an entry. The pools are capped at 64 each. pruneParameterProposals/pruneReassignments only drop entries whose sequence or value guard no longer matches current state (governance.go:229-236) — a voteless entry bound to the current sequence/digest (or to balance 0 of some unknown key) is NEVER pruned. Once 64 junk entries fill a pool, a legitimate proposal is a new key and is refused by the >=64 cap, so it never pools or gossips. The governance sequence can only advance via a pooled certificate reaching quorum, which can no longer happen — permanent deadlock. All endpoints are unauthenticated (httptransport.go:186-205); GET /hdls/governance hands the attacker the current sequence/digest to bind.
findings.failure_scenario: An attacker who can reach the node port (no key needed) reads GET /hdls/governance, then POSTs 64 distinct voteless ParameterChanges (each an Acceptable profile binding the current digest+sequence) to /hdls/parameter-vote and 64 voteless Reassignments (distinct unknown accounts, prev=0) to /hdls/reassignment-vote — 128 small requests per node. Both pools are now full of un-prunable junk. A legitimate validator's genuine vote for a fee change or a reassignment is refused at the >=64 cap, never pools, never gossips, never enacts. Governance is frozen for the life of the network. PoC: a quorum-1 validator's fully-valid fee change AND reassignment never enact after the squat; pools stay 64/64 across 15 blocks.
findings.attacker: anyone who can reach the node's HTTP port (unauthenticated; no validator key)
findings.known_status: Relates to deferred #10 (unauthenticated write API / rate limiting), but is a distinct logic flaw, not just a volumetric concern: entries are pooled before verification and the cap+no-eviction makes a single 128-request burst a PERMANENT freeze that rate-limiting alone does not fix. New angle / materially worse than #10 as recorded.
findings.poc: <scratch>/governance/node/zz_govreview_poc_test.go (TestPoCGovPoolSquatFreezesGovernance) — FAILs: GOVERNANCE FROZEN, quorum-1 change+reassignment never enact
findings.fix: Do not pool a proposal until it carries at least one VERIFIED current-validator vote; key/evict by whether progress is possible; or reserve capacity / use a per-sender bound. At minimum, drop pooled entries that have made no progress and never pool a voteless certificate.

findings.title: Slashing does not durably burn a proven double-signer's validating or governance power
findings.description: The owner's principle is 'two different signings means the key is burned'. It does not hold. applySlashes (block.go:72-89) deletes only the offender's OWN account. (1) Dynamic + delegated: deriveValidators (validators.go:31-61) sums each account's balance by its ValidatorNode; depositors delegating to a bank keep their own accounts, so a slashed bank keeps nearly all its voting power and stays a validator — directly contradicting docs/consensus.md 'removes the offender's account ... ejecting them from a dynamic set'. (2) Dynamic + self-staked: the offender is ejected, but node.commit (node.go:649-654) prunes its evidence the moment it leaves the set, so a single later incoming payment re-creates the account (ValidatorNode defaults to self in ProcessPayments) and re-admits the key — nobody re-slashes it. (3) Static set: the set is config; slashing confiscates the balance but the key keeps FULL consensus + governance voting power forever. In every mode a burned key keeps or regains power.
findings.failure_scenario: Dynamic/delegated: a 'bank' validator B (own balance 1, 200 delegated to it) equivocates and is slashed. On every node B's derived power is still 200 of 400 — above the skip threshold, able to veto or help ratify. B keeps casting consensus votes and ⅔ governance votes (parameter/reassignment) that count. PoC confirms B remains in the set post-slash. Static: PoC shows a slashed key still supplies the DECIDING governance vote (3-of-4) to mint 1,000,000 to an attacker account after its own slash. Self-staked: PoC shows an ejected key back in the set one 20-unit payment later. The compromise-exclusion the eMudhra retrospective wants is absent.
findings.attacker: a single validator whose key is proven compromised/equivocating (the exact party slashing targets)
findings.known_status: New. docs/consensus.md and managing-the-currency.md present slashing as THE accountability lever and claim ejection from a dynamic set; the code achieves durable ejection in no mode. Includes a docs-drift component (consensus.md 'ejecting them from a dynamic set').
findings.poc: node: <scratch>/governance/node/zz_govreview_poc_test.go (TestPoCGovSlashDoesNotBurnDynamicValidatorKey) — FAILs on delegated-still-validating and re-admit-by-payment. ledger: <scratch>/governance/ledger/zz_govreview_poc_test.go (TestPoCGovSlashedStaticValidatorStillRatifies) — FAILs: burned key casts the deciding governance vote
findings.fix: Tombstone slashed keys in committed state (a durable burn-set under the digest): exclude a tombstoned key from deriveValidators and from the static set's effective power, reject its votes/certificates, and refuse to re-create or re-fund it. Keep evidence actionable against a recreated key (retire the 'prune once it leaves the set' step for tombstoning).

findings.title: A departed voter's stuck pool vote poisons a proposal so a clear live quorum can never carry it
findings.description: ParameterChange.Valid / Reassignment.Valid reject the WHOLE certificate if ANY carried vote is from a key not in the current validator set (governance.go:79, reassignment.go:97). The node's pools accumulate votes by validator and never remove one (governance.go:55-71); addParameterVotes dedups but cannot drop a vote, and pruning only deletes a whole entry on a sequence/value change. So if a validator votes for a pooled proposal and then leaves the set (re-delegates, drops below the dynamic threshold, or is slashed), its signature stays wedged in that pooled certificate. pendingParameterChange calls Valid on the pooled entry, which now always returns false, so the proposal can never be carried — even though the remaining CURRENT validators hold a clear >⅔. The admin view still shows it 'ready ✓'. Re-submitting the good votes is a no-op (same pool key, already-voted). A fresh clean entry can't be created (key occupied).
findings.failure_scenario: Dynamic set v1(60) v2(30) v3(15). Small validator v3 votes for a fee change, then re-delegates its stake to v1 (one signed account update) — leaving the set. v1 and v2 (now 105 of 105 power, well above quorum 71) both vote. The pooled certificate is [v3,v1,v2]; Valid hits v3 (not a current validator) and returns false, so pendingParameterChange returns nil and the change is never proposed, despite a 105/71 live quorum. PoC: votedPower=105, reached=true, amendsCurrent=true, yet pendingParameterChange()=false; a fresh [v1,v2] certificate is Valid=true but cannot be pooled. A minority validator can thus veto any proposal it voted on by moving its stake once; ordinary validator churn/slashing wedges in-flight proposals silently.
findings.attacker: one minority validator (griefing), or ordinary non-adversarial validator-set churn/slashing
findings.known_status: New. Not in findings.md/TODO.md; distinct from the C5 deterministic-selection fix (that was about map order, this is about stale votes never being evicted).
findings.poc: <scratch>/governance/node/zz_govreview_poc_test.go (TestPoCGovDepartedVoterPoisonsPooledProposal) — FAILs: votedPower 105 of quorum 71, reached=true, but pendingParameterChange()=false
findings.fix: When building/validating a pooled certificate, filter its votes to current validators (drop non-members) rather than rejecting the whole certificate, and prune votes from departed validators each commit. Re-tally the surviving current-validator votes against the quorum.

findings.title: Governance certificates and payments replay across a re-genesis (sequence and BlockID reset, networkId reused)
findings.description: The only replay anchors for governance are the GovernanceSequence (parameters.go:198) and, for payments, BlockID. Both are chain-local and restart at 0/height-1 when a node boots fresh (node.go:98,128). The vote/payment preimages are bound to networkId but NOT to any genesis identifier. operating-a-network.md:136-171 documents re-genesis as the normal path for ANY release that changes the state digest or signing preimage ('restart every node on the new version from the captured state'), reusing the SAME networkId and validator keys and re-asserting balances. On the reseeded chain every old certificate/payment every node pooled or gossiped is signature-valid again at its old sequence/BlockID; it applies whenever its value guard matches (a prev=0 newcomer grant matches immediately if the grantee holds 0). The doc says only 'the cryptography (and the genesis hash) change' — but a plain software upgrade keeps the scheme and networkId, so nothing stops the replay.
findings.failure_scenario: On the old chain, seq 0 grants a newcomer 500; the newcomer later spends it. The community does a documented software-upgrade re-genesis from the captured state (same networkId, same keys). On the new chain the GovernanceSequence starts at 0 again. Anyone holding the old grant certificate (it was gossiped network-wide) resubmits it verbatim; it is Valid at sequence 0 (newcomer holds 0 on the new chain) and re-mints 500 with no new vote. PoC also shows the old height-2 payment replaying at height 2 of the new chain. Supply inflates by every historically-ratified grant and every re-submittable old payment.
findings.attacker: anyone retaining an old-chain certificate or payment (all nodes pooled/gossiped them), after an operator-run re-genesis
findings.known_status: New. The within-chain cycle replay is correctly closed by the sequence (verified: TestReassignmentSequenceGuardBlocksCycleReplay, TestChaosGovernanceCycleReplayStaysInert). This is the CROSS-genesis reset the sequence does not cover; the re-genesis procedure in operating-a-network.md does not warn of it (docs-drift component).
findings.poc: <scratch>/governance/ledger/zz_govreview_poc_test.go (TestPoCGovCertificateReplaysAcrossReGenesis) — FAILs: old grant re-mints 500 and old payment replays on the reseeded chain
findings.fix: Bind a genesis identifier (genesis digest / an epoch counter) into every signed preimage (votes and payments), or mandate a fresh networkId on every re-genesis and say so prominently in operating-a-network.md. Then old signatures are invalid on the new chain.

findings.title: Unauthenticated governance vote stalls the single event loop ~9s via big.Rat exponent amplification
findings.description: Governance amounts travel as JSON strings parsed into *big.Rat. big.Rat.SetString accepts exponent notation, so the ~12-byte string '1p10000000' decodes (~2ms) to a 10-Mbit integer whose RatString() costs ~1.8s. parameterVoteFields/reassignmentVoteFields (governance.go:31-35, reassignment.go:265-273) call RatString to build the preimage, and this happens BEFORE signature verification: VerifyParameterVote/VerifyReassignmentVote receive the preimage as an already-evaluated argument (node/governance.go:64, reassignment.go:302), and addParameterVotes only dedups POOLED voters — so one message can repeat a (public) validator key thousands of times, each triggering a RatString, before any bad signature is rejected. All of this runs on the single event-loop goroutine (node.go:289-296). The pooled entry (GOV-3) then re-stringifies on EVERY startHeight via pendingParameterChange→Valid. Unlike the recorded 1MiB/ApplyBlock DoS, a ~500-byte packet suffices and the damage persists.
findings.failure_scenario: Attacker (no key) reads GET /hdls/governance for the current digest/sequence, then POSTs a 521-byte ParameterChange whose NewParameters.TransactionCost is '1p10000000' and whose Votes repeat the public validator key 3x with empty signatures. PoC: the event loop stalls ~9s (~2.25s per carried vote); a 1MiB body holds ~14,000 such votes → ~8.8 hours of single-loop stall from one request. The entry then pools (binds current sequence/digest, never pruned) and every height re-processes it: observed block rate collapses from 64 to 2 per 2s and stays there. Repeatable/stackable → sustained throughput denial of the whole node from tiny unauthenticated packets.
findings.attacker: anyone who can reach the node's HTTP port (unauthenticated)
findings.known_status: Strengthens deferred #10 and the recorded MEDIUM 'unauthenticated write API + single-loop serialization'. New angle: specific amplification (RatString on attacker rationals, pre-verification, repeated per carried vote and per height) makes it a ~500-byte PERSISTENT stall, materially worse than the 1MiB one-shot recorded.
findings.poc: <scratch>/governance/node/zz_govreview_poc_test.go (TestPoCGovHugeRationalStallsEventLoop) — FAILs: 9.02s loop stall, block rate 64→2 per 2s
findings.fix: Verify the signature before building the RatString preimage (or bound the serialized size / numerator+denominator bit-length of a submitted amount at intake, and reject exponent notation); dedup a message's carried voters before verifying; and apply GOV-3's don't-pool-until-verified fix.

checked_ok: Governance sequence correctly blocks the within-chain value-cycle replay (A→B→A then replay A→B stays inert) — ledger TestReassignmentSequenceGuardBlocksCycleReplay and node TestChaosGovernanceCycleReplayStaysInert both pass; GOV-6 is specifically the cross-re-genesis reset the sequence cannot cover

At-most-one-governance-action-per-block is enforced: ProposeBlock prefers the parameter change, and ApplyBlock (block.go:211) rejects a block carrying both a ParameterChange and a Reassignment (they would bind the same sequence)

ParameterChange.Valid / Reassignment.Valid correctly require each vote to be a DISTINCT CURRENT validator (seen map + Contains) and combined power >= Quorum (strict >⅔); unknown-validator and double-counted votes are rejected
The non-negative reassignment guard holds (NewAmount.Sign()<0 rejected) and nil validator set / nil amounts are rejected

Every governed field is under both the committed digest and the vote preimage: LedgerParameters.fields() covers TransactionCost, BlockIntervalMs, StepTimeoutMs, MaxPeers, MaxMessageBytes, and LedgerState.Digest folds in the GovernanceSequence — no governed field is omitted from the digest

proposalKey/reassignmentKey key the FULL proposed profile + previous digest + sequence (the C5 fix), so two proposals sharing only a cost pool separately; pendingParameterChange/pendingReassignment scan sorted keys (deterministic)

MinMessageBytes floor is enforced in Acceptable and at config load, so governance cannot vote the message cap below a payable size (the one timing/size field that IS brick-proofed — unlike the interval/timeout of GOV-2)
Negative transaction cost is refused at config load (config.go:88) and clamped to zero in ProcessPayments, and Acceptable rejects it — the C3 mint class stays closed

Reassignment vote preimage binds the raw account key (not a name), so a dishonest node cannot retarget a reassignment at vote-collection time; the ⅔ quorum only forms if voters independently signed the same key+amounts

ApplyBlock re-verifies every governance certificate against the validator set independently of ProposeBlock, and recomputes the result digest — a proposer cannot smuggle an unratified change past honest nodes
notes:
Burned-key matrix (GOV-4) — does a proven double-signer keep power after slashing?

| validator mode | offender's own account | effective voting power after slash | re-entry |
|---|---|---|---|
| static set (config) | balance confiscated | UNCHANGED — full consensus + governance power forever (set is config, slash can't touch it) | n/a (never left) |
| dynamic, self-staked | deleted | drops to 0, ejected | one incoming payment re-creates the account (ValidatorNode defaults to self) and re-admits it; evidence already pruned, so no re-slash |
| dynamic, delegated ("bank") | deleted (tiny) | KEEPS ~all delegated power — stays a validator (contradicts docs/consensus.md "ejecting them from a dynamic set") | never left |

In no mode is the key durably burned, so the owner's "two different signings means the key is burned" principle is unmet. A tombstone set under the state digest (exclude from derivation AND from the static set's effective power, refuse re-funding/re-admission, keep evidence actionable against a recreated key) is the single fix that makes it hold in all three modes.

area: NODE TRUST ANCHORS — onboarding, catch-up, snapshot and backup (node/sync.go, node/persist.go, node/node.go, node/peerdns.go, node/topology.go, cmd/server/config.go)
summary: The adoption plumbing is mostly solid: all three paths (adopt, catchUp, loadSnapshot) gate on a real >2/3 Commit.Verify, bind the commit to the full LedgerState digest (accounts+params+governance sequence), enforce strict height monotonicity (never roll back), reject other-network snapshots via network-bound vote signatures, and the going-forward validator set is re-derived from verified state. Peer DNS correctly uses only CURRENT validators' addresses, so a flood of non-validator accounts cannot eclipse. BUT the trust ANCHOR for any fresh or (re)starting node is the GENESIS validator set, permanently and with no weak-subjectivity pin — which is exactly the eMudhra blind spot. An attacker holding >1/3 (by genesis power) of the genesis validators' keys — keys that may have LEFT the active set (zero stake, nothing to slash, invisible to live consensus) or been weakly generated — can forge a fully attacker-controlled checkpoint that a joiner adopts (SYNC-1, HIGH). The owner's "two signings burns the key" principle cannot fire because the forgery is shown only to the victim, never to the live network. The same genesis-anchoring, flipped, permanently bricks onboarding/recovery once the set rotates fully past the founders (SYNC-3). Separately, the catch-up client reads a peer's checkpoint with no size bound (SYNC-2).

findings.title: Long-range checkpoint forgery: joiners trust genesis validator keys forever (no weak subjectivity)
findings.description: A fresh or restarting node anchors checkpoint trust on the GENESIS validator set forever: bestCheckpoint passes cfg.Genesis (sync.go:98), adopt/loadSnapshot pass pre-start n.accounts (=genesis). verifyCheckpoint accepts any checkpoint whose Commit is a >2/3 quorum of the PEER-SUPPLIED signing set (cp.Validators, dynamic mode) and whose signers cover >1/3 of the genesis anchor's power. cp.Validators is never cross-checked against what cp.Accounts would derive. So an attacker holding >1/3 (by genesis power) of the GENESIS validators' private keys can fabricate arbitrary accounts, advertise those same keys as the signing set, self-sign the commit, and the joiner adopts attacker-controlled state. Those genesis keys may have left the active set (zero current stake, not slashable, ignored by live consensus) or been weakly generated (eMudhra). There is no weak-subjectivity checkpoint or pinning to retire the anchor.
findings.failure_scenario: Dynamic-validator village. Founders A,B,C leave over a year; their old laptops/keys are discarded or were weakly generated. Attacker recovers A,B's keys (2 of 3 = >1/3). It builds a checkpoint at height 100: accounts crediting itself 9e9 (founders at 0), Validators=[A,B], a 2-of-2 self-signed commit over that digest. A new merchant node (or a founder's rebuilt node) boots with the original genesis config, polls a peer/attacker, verifyCheckpoint returns true, fastForward adopts it: the node now believes the attacker's balance and height. 'Two signings burns the key' never triggers — the forged commit is shown only to the victim, so the live network sees no equivocation and the keys hold no stake to slash.
findings.attacker: holder of >1/3 (by genesis power) of the former/weak genesis validators' stolen or cracked keys
findings.known_status: new — findings.md calls onboarding 'sound ... with the full-rotation limit documented, not glossed'; no prior round considered compromise of FORMER/weak anchor keys (the eMudhra lens). Not deferred #7 (ledger height) or #10 (open API).
findings.poc: <scratch>/sync-trust/node/synctrust_poc_test.go — TestPoCLongRangeCheckpointForgeryAcceptedByJoiner and TestPoCLongRangeNeedsOnlyOverOneThirdOfGenesisKeys: both PASS, printing that a genesis-anchored joiner accepts and adopts (height 101, attacker balance 9e9) a checkpoint signed only by former/abandoned keys, with 2-of-3 keys sufficing; the same checkpoint is rejected against a live-set anchor.
findings.fix: Add a weak-subjectivity pin: let operators configure a recent trusted (height, stateDigest) and its validator-set hash, refreshed out-of-band, and anchor verifyCheckpoint to that instead of genesis for joiners — so abandoned genesis keys cannot authorise a checkpoint past the pin. Defense-in-depth: require cp.Validators to equal deriveValidators(cp.Accounts) in dynamic mode so a peer cannot advertise an arbitrary signing set. Document that the anchor keys are a root of trust that must stay secure (and be re-pinned when founders leave).

findings.title: Full validator rotation past genesis permanently bricks onboarding and crash-recovery
findings.description: The flip side of SYNC-1. Because the joiner/restart anchor is always the genesis set, verifyCheckpoint's >1/3-overlap test (vouched*3 > trusted.TotalPower) fails once the live validator set has rotated fully past the genesis validators — even for a perfectly honest, >2/3-signed, digest-bound current checkpoint. bestCheckpoint fetches exactly ONE checkpoint per peer; there is no bisection/chain-walk and no weak-subjectivity pin, so the 'chain of intermediate checkpoints to walk' that consensus.md:126-128 says would be needed does not exist. A node also re-verifies its OWN on-disk snapshot against genesis (persist.go:31), so after rotation it cannot even reload its own state and falls back to genesis (height 1), then cannot catch up either. Onboarding and recovery silently break for good.
findings.failure_scenario: A long-lived village currency: over time the 8 founding laptops are all replaced and the founders' accounts drop below the validator threshold, so none of the genesis validators remain in the live set. Everything runs fine for existing up-to-date nodes (their catch-up anchor tracks the live set). Then someone adds a new node, or a running node crashes and restarts: it boots on the original genesis config, fetches the current honest checkpoint, verifyCheckpoint rejects it (zero genesis overlap), and the node sits stuck at genesis forever. No error explains why; there is no documented knob to move the anchor forward.
findings.attacker: no attacker — triggered by ordinary validator rotation over the network's lifetime
findings.known_status: sharper angle on the 'full-rotation limit' findings.md calls 'documented, not glossed': shown here to be a hard onboarding/recovery brick with no implemented bisection or pin, and to also block reloading a node's OWN snapshot — materially worse than a mere note.
findings.poc: <scratch>/sync-trust/node/synctrust_poc_test.go — TestPoCFullRotationBricksOnboarding: PASS. A genuine >2/3-signed current checkpoint signed by a fully-rotated set (X,Y,Z; founder A below threshold) is rejected by a genesis-anchored joiner.
findings.fix: Implement the weak-subjectivity pin from SYNC-1 (also the fix here): a periodically-refreshed trusted recent checkpoint lets joiners/restarts anchor to the live-ish set. Alternatively implement the documented checkpoint bisection (walk intermediate checkpoints so each step overlaps the previous anchor). Persist the last-trusted signing-set hash alongside the snapshot so a node can at least reload its own state. Until then, document loudly that replacing all genesis validators disables onboarding/recovery.

findings.title: Catch-up checkpoint fetch has no response-size bound (memory DoS)
findings.description: fetchCheckpoint reads a peer's /hdls/checkpoint reply with a bare json.NewDecoder(resp.Body).Decode(&cp) and no size limit (sync.go:115), while the node's own server intake caps every request body at 1 MiB via http.MaxBytesReader (httptransport.go:308). catchUpLoop polls catch-up sources every few seconds (sync.go:38-55) and bestCheckpoint fetches from each. A malicious source can stream an arbitrarily large (or slow) body within the 5s client timeout, forcing the polling node to allocate it into memory, repeatedly. For a node with no bootstrap configured, catch-up sources are its gossip peers = the on-chain validator addresses (peerdns.go), so a single validator that publishes its Address becomes a source — one dishonest validator can memory-pressure its peers, which the BFT model should tolerate.
findings.failure_scenario: A validator (dynamic mode) publishes an on-chain Address pointing at an attacker-controlled HTTP server (or a bootstrap operator turns malicious). Victim nodes without bootstrap peers resolve that address as a catch-up source and poll /hdls/checkpoint every few seconds. The server answers each poll with a multi-hundred-MB JSON body (streamed fast for <5s). Each victim decodes the whole thing into a Checkpoint, spiking RSS on the single event-loop machine on every tick; sustained, it drives nodes to OOM or GC thrash while honest traffic starves. No signature or verification runs until AFTER the full body is decoded, so the cost is paid before any check.
findings.attacker: one validator (via a published on-chain address) or any configured bootstrap/sync peer
findings.known_status: new — distinct from deferred #10 (open mutating endpoints + event-loop DoS, guarded by the 1 MiB intake bound and server timeouts): this is the CLIENT-side checkpoint read, a different code path not covered by fronting the server with a TLS/rate-limit proxy.
findings.poc: <scratch>/sync-trust/node/synctrust_poc_test.go — TestPoCUnboundedCheckpointFetch: PASS. An httptest server returns a 4 MiB checkpoint (4x the 1 MiB server bound); fetchCheckpoint decodes it with no error and the full oversized field survives, proving no cap.
findings.fix: Wrap the response body in an io.LimitReader (or set resp.Body via a MaxBytesReader-equivalent) with a generous but bounded cap sized for the largest legitimate account set, mirroring the 1 MiB server intake; reject and move on if exceeded. Consider a configurable max-checkpoint-bytes and bounding bestCheckpoint's total work per tick.

findings.title: Docs claim onboarding is 'safe even from an untrusted bootstrap peer' without the weak-subjectivity caveat
findings.description: consensus.md states a joiner is 'safe even from an untrusted bootstrap peer' and that 'an honest anchored validator only signs valid commits, and a fabricated all-stranger set has no anchor overlap and is rejected'; operating-a-network.md says 'the bootstrap peer does not have to be trusted.' These are true only under an unstated assumption the code bakes in: that the ANCHOR (genesis) validators' keys remain honest and uncompromised forever, including after those validators leave the active set. SYNC-1 shows that assumption is the whole vulnerability — abandoned or weakly-generated genesis keys (the eMudhra case) still authorise any checkpoint for a joiner. The docs present certificate verification as the complete trust story and omit that the trust ultimately reduces to those specific keys staying secure for the network's whole life.
findings.failure_scenario: An operator reads 'the bootstrap peer does not have to be trusted' and 'safe even from an untrusted bootstrap peer', concludes onboarding needs no special key hygiene, and treats retired founder keys casually (deletes backups carelessly, reuses hardware, never re-pins). An attacker later recovers or finds a set of those retired keys and forges checkpoints per SYNC-1. The operator had no warning from the docs that the retired genesis keys were still a live root of trust.
findings.attacker: no attacker — documentation gap
findings.known_status: new docs-drift, the documentation face of SYNC-1; findings.md's doc spot-checks did not cover the onboarding trust-assumption wording.
findings.poc: none — documentation claim; the underlying code behavior is proven by the SYNC-1 PoC in <scratch>/sync-trust/node/synctrust_poc_test.go.
findings.fix: State plainly that onboarding trust rests on the anchor (genesis, or a configured weak-subjectivity pin) validator keys staying uncompromised for the network's lifetime; that retired/founder keys remain a root of trust for joiners until a pin moves the anchor forward; and that losing/leaking >1/3 of them lets an attacker forge checkpoints for new or rebooting nodes. Tie the guidance to the planned pin/bisection fix.

checked_ok: All three adoption paths (adopt node.go:327, catchUp node.go:357, loadSnapshot persist.go:16) call verifyCheckpoint, which requires a real >2/3 Commit.Verify of the signing set before fastForward — no path adopts state without the quorum it claims (brief point 6).

verifyCheckpoint binds the commit to the FULL state: LedgerState{Accounts,Parameters,GovernanceSequence}.Digest() == cp.Commit.BlockDigest (node.go:392) — tampered/truncated accounts, params or sequence are rejected.

Height monotonicity enforced on every path: adopt/catchUp/loadSnapshot all return early when cp.Commit.Height+1 <= n.height (node.go:331, 361; persist.go:28) — a stale checkpoint cannot roll a node back.

Cross-network snapshots/checkpoints are rejected: commit votes are verified with cfg.NetworkID and the network is bound into each vote's signing preimage, so votes signed for another network fail Verify.
Going-forward validator set is re-derived from verified state (startHeight -> validatorsFor(n.accounts), node.go:472); cp.Validators is used only to verify the adopting commit, not kept as authority.
Snapshot write is crash-safe (writeAtomic fsyncs temp then dir, persist.go:73-96); a parse failure or verify failure on load is ignored and the node starts at genesis rather than adopting garbage.
BackupPath mirror writes the identical verified Checkpoint JSON; on load it goes through loadSnapshot's certificate verification like any snapshot — the backup is not a separate trust bypass.

Peer DNS uses only CURRENT validators' published addresses (resolvedPeerAddresses, peerdns.go:30 filters currentValidators.Contains) — a flood of non-validator accounts claiming addresses cannot influence peer selection or eclipse a node.

Topology neighbor selection (Neighbors/toCoord/fromCoord) is deterministic over sorted validator keys; eclipse would require validator-level stake AND key-grinding into a victim's Hamming-graph positions, and relay is trusted only to relay (signatures protect safety), so the damage ceiling is censorship/liveness, not fund theft.
cmd/server/config.go load() validates key lengths, non-negative cost, and genesis Acceptable() (C3/C4 fixes intact); bootstrap/snapshot/backup paths are plumbed through unchanged.
The >1/3 anchor-overlap arithmetic (vouched*3 > trusted.TotalPower, node.go:400) is correct for the BFT skipping rule and does not overflow for any realistic set.

area: NODE UNTRUSTED-INPUT BOUNDARY (node/httptransport.go, node/node.go event loop, mempool/updatepool, relay, governance/reassignment intake, cmd/server)
summary: The intake boundary is mostly disciplined: payments and account-updates are signature-verified before admission/relay, checkpoints are quorum-verified off-loop before touching the event loop, far-future heights/rounds are dropped (onProposal height gate, ReceiveVote maxRoundLookahead), proposals are proposer-authenticated, and the mempool/update pools are size-bounded and content-deduped. But three cheap, unauthenticated amplification/state-growth vectors earlier rounds missed survive, all reachable by anyone who can reach the port (the documented trust boundary): (1) a ~60-byte payment whose Amount is an exponent literal like "1e1000000" expands to a 3.3M-bit rational and burns ~100-150ms of single-event-loop time per request via big.Rat RatString/Marshal — slipping entirely under the 1 MiB body bound that security.md claims prevents JSON DoS; (2) consensus votes are relayed and stored in heightVotes before any signature/validator check, so junk is amplified to every peer and grows an uncapped map; (3) governance vote pools create a slot before verifying any vote, letting 64 vote-less junk proposals permanently brick parameter/reassignment voting. The /hdls/resolve answer is anchored to a committed digest but not provably bound to it, and the documented "compare digests across nodes" cross-check is weaker than claimed. All four are code-fixable and extend deferred #10 with concrete new angles. No mint/steal/fork vector was found at this boundary.

findings.title: Tiny exponent-form big.Rat amounts cause superlinear per-request work on the single event loop (1 MiB body bound does not bound the work)
findings.description: Payment.Amount is a *big.Rat decoded from attacker JSON. big.Rat.UnmarshalText accepts exponent form, so the ~10-byte literal "1e1000000" (body ~60 bytes, far under the 1 MiB MaxBytesReader at httptransport.go:308) expands to a 3.3M-bit rational. admitPayment runs ON THE EVENT LOOP and pays superlinear big.Rat cost regardless of config: WithinMessageBound→json.Marshal (block.go:21) when MaxMessageBytes>0, and mem.contains→PaymentID→RatString (payment.go:46) when it is 0. Measured ~135ms (bound=2000) / ~91ms (bound=0) vs ~70us normal — a >1000x amplification of serialized loop time from a cheap, replayable, self-signed request needing no balance or validator slot. Same vector via ParameterChange.NewParameters.TransactionCost (proposalKey→Digest→RatString, governance.go:18) and Reassignment amounts (reassignmentKey, reassignment.go:15), both before any auth.
findings.failure_scenario: Attacker signs one Payment{PublicKeyFrom: own key, Amount: "1e1000000", BlockID: huge} and POSTs it to /hdls/pay (or /hdls/payment) repeatedly. VerifyPayment passes (own key). Each request enqueues onto the loop; admitPayment spends ~100-150ms marshalling/RatStringing the expanded rational before refusing it. A few requests/second saturate the single consensus goroutine, stalling block production network-wide for the duration of the flood. security.md's "Bounded request bodies ... avoiding the unbounded-JSON DoS" guarantee does not hold.
findings.attacker: anyone reaching the port
findings.known_status: Extends deferred #10 (unauthenticated-API single-loop DoS) and GLM C6 (big.Rat JSON footgun, rated 'non-exploitable today'). New angle: the amplification is ~60 bytes -> ~150ms of serialized loop work, replayable, and it defeats the specific in-process guard #10 named as residual (the 1 MiB body bound) and the governed MaxMessageBytes cap. Materially worse and code-fixable, not just 'rate-limit the port'.
findings.poc: <scratch>/node-input/node/zz_poc_test.go (TestPoCHugeAmountStallsEventLoop) — PASS, logs normal=~70us vs huge=~135ms (bound=2000) and ~91ms (bound=0)
findings.fix: At intake, bound the decoded amount's magnitude cheaply before any RatString/Marshal — e.g. reject a Payment/TransactionCost/Reassignment amount whose Num().BitLen()+Denom().BitLen() exceeds a small cap (a few thousand bits covers any real balance). Do it in admitPayment, addParameterVotes, addReassignmentVotes and VerifyPayment's callers, and correct security.md's 'bounded bodies' claim to 'bounded decoded magnitude'.

findings.title: Consensus votes are relayed and stored (heightVotes) before any signature/validator check — junk amplification + unbounded map
findings.description: handleVote (httptransport.go:139) decodes a Vote and calls SubmitVote with no verification — unlike handleGossipPayment (:156) and handleAccountUpdate (:175), which verify signatures first. In evVote (node.go:268) the node unconditionally rememberVote()s the vote into heightVotes (node.go:552, keyed by attacker-controlled Validator+Signature, NO size cap — the mempool has one, this map does not) and relay()s it to every peer (node.go:273). The driver's VoteSet.Add verifies only for TALLYING and silently drops non-validators/bad signatures, but relay and heightVotes storage happen regardless. So the 'verify before acting' rule the brief requires is violated for the relay/remember actions. reGossipVotes (node.go:562) then re-broadcasts the entire heightVotes set to all peers every timeout tick.
findings.failure_scenario: Attacker reads the live height from GET /hdls/status, then floods POST /hdls/vote with distinct junk Votes (Height=current, random Validator/Signature strings). Each is relayed once to all P peers (1->P amplification) and stored in heightVotes; the uncapped map grows for the whole commit window, and every re-gossip tick re-floods the entire junk set to all peers. If the loop is also stalled (e.g. via NODE-IN-1) the map never resets and grows until OOM. Non-validator, no key, no stake required.
findings.attacker: anyone reaching the port
findings.known_status: New. Within deferred #10's area but a distinct code defect: votes are the ONLY intake path that relays/persists before verifying (payments/updates/governance votes all verify first), and heightVotes is the only intake-fed map with no size bound. A front-door rate limiter does not stop the 1->P amplification or the per-tick re-gossip of each admitted junk vote.
findings.poc: <scratch>/node-input/node/zz_poc_test.go (TestPoCUnauthenticatedVoteFloodAmplifiesAndGrows) — PASS: 5000 unverified junk votes, all relayed, all stored in heightVotes, all re-gossiped per tick
findings.fix: In evVote, only rememberVote/relay a vote that passes v.Verify(scheme,networkID) AND heightVals.Contains(v.Validator) (cheap: ~50us Ed25519), mirroring the payment/update handlers. Add a size cap to heightVotes (validator count is the natural bound once membership is checked).

findings.title: Governance vote pools create a proposal slot before verifying any vote — unauthenticated 64-slot fill permanently bricks parameter/reassignment voting
findings.description: handleParameterVote/handleReassignmentVote are unauthenticated. addParameterVotes (governance.go:41) checks only NewParameters.Acceptable, then CREATES the pool entry (governance.go:52-53) before iterating/verifying any carried vote; a change with zero valid votes still occupies a slot. The pool is capped at 64 (governance.go:49), so once full, a genuine validator's valid vote for a new proposal is refused (return false, not pooled, not relayed, not counted). addReassignmentVotes (reassignment.go:43) is the same and has no Acceptable gate at all. GET /hdls/governance exposes the current parameters and GovernanceSequence, so an attacker sets PreviousParametersDigest/Sequence to the current values and the junk entries survive commit-time pruning (pruneParameterProposals/pruneReassignments only drop stale-digest/sequence entries).
findings.failure_scenario: Attacker POSTs 64 distinct, vote-less ParameterChange messages (varying BlockIntervalMs; PreviousParametersDigest=current, Sequence=current) to /hdls/parameter-vote on each node. Pools fill to 64 and survive pruning. Every subsequent genuine validator parameter-change vote is refused at intake, so no proposal ever reaches quorum and no proposer can carry one — governance (fee changes, reassignments/grants) is bricked until nodes restart, whereupon the attacker refills (64 tiny requests/node).
findings.attacker: anyone reaching the port
findings.known_status: New. Within deferred #10's area but a specific create-before-verify defect with a concrete governance-liveness impact and a persistence (pruning-evasion) twist that #10's generic 'rate-limit the port' framing does not capture.
findings.poc: <scratch>/node-input/node/zz_poc_test.go (TestPoCGovernancePoolFillBlocksLegitVotes) — PASS: 64 vote-less junk proposals fill + survive pruning; a real validator's valid vote is refused
findings.fix: Do not allocate a pool entry until at least one carried vote verifies as a current validator (move the create below the vote loop, or require >=1 verified vote before insertion). Count the 64 cap over proposals that hold >=1 verified validator vote.

findings.title: /hdls/resolve answer is not provably bound to its digest; documented cross-check (compare digests) is insufficient, and Height is off by one
findings.description: handleResolve returns a record (name, publicKey, address, description) read from committed accounts plus StateDigest=hex(snap.Decided) and Height=snap.Height. The fields are genuinely under that digest (Address was added to StateDigest by fix #4). But the answer carries NO commit certificate and NO inclusion proof, and the node simply asserts the 32-byte digest string. The ResolveRecord comment (:257) and operating-a-network.md:198 tell a distrustful client to 'query K nodes and compare — matching digests mean the same ⅔-agreed state'. That is weaker than claimed: a single dishonest node can return a fabricated record alongside the honest digest string it copied from others, and a client comparing only digests is fooled. The sound check is to compare the actual key/address FIELDS across nodes (which honest nodes agree on precisely because Address is in the digest). Also Height=snap.Height is the in-progress height (committed+1), while the digest finalizes committed height snap.Height-1.
findings.failure_scenario: A client follows the docs and resolves alice via its reference node, comparing the returned stateDigest against a couple of other nodes. The reference node returns {address: attacker-controlled, publicKey: alice, stateDigest: <value copied from honest nodes>}. All digests match, so the client concludes the answer is ⅔-agreed and uses the attacker's address (e.g. for peer/endpoint discovery). Impact is bounded for payments (the wallet pays by ToName, resolved on-chain at apply time — ui/wallet.go), so this is address/display integrity, not fund redirection.
findings.attacker: one dishonest reference node
findings.known_status: New (answers the brief's resolve question). Builds on fix #4 (Address now in the digest), which makes the correct cross-check possible but is not what the docs instruct.
findings.poc: none — mechanism is evident from httptransport.go:270-300 (no certificate/inclusion proof served; digest is an unverified node assertion) and the wallet pay-by-name path (ui/wallet.go:216-222) bounding impact; rated low/high-confidence without a failing test.
findings.fix: Either serve the Commit certificate (and ideally an inclusion proof) with the resolve answer so a client can verify the record against a ⅔ quorum, or correct the docs to say clients must compare the actual publicKey/address fields across independent nodes (digest equality alone is insufficient). Separately, label Height as the committed height the digest finalizes (snap.Height-1) or rename the field.

handleAccountUpdate (httptransport.go:175) verifies the owner signature before SubmitUpdate/relay; evUpdate also enforces WithinMessageBound before relay (node.go:286)

area: WALLET + ADMIN UI (ui/ module: main.go, wallet.go, keyfile.go, admin.go, templates/*.html)
summary: The wallet is well-structured and several prior findings are genuinely fixed (html/template is used so on-chain strings auto-escape; receipt verification checks signature+PaymentID+validator-membership; the CSRF guard blocks ordinary cross-site/same-site browser POSTs; the hand-rolled PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA256 matches the stdlib on 300 randomized vectors incl. >block-size passwords and multi-block output). But the localhost-only, auto-signing design leans entirely on the origin guard and on key-at-rest sealing, and both have gaps. The headline is a DNS-rebinding bypass of the CSRF guard (KEY-1, high): the guard compares Origin.Host==r.Host rather than a fixed expected host, so after a rebind a web page the user merely visits can drive signed payments and governance votes with the local key — exactly the "key does harm without being leaked" shape the owner is worried about. On the key-at-rest side, following the tool's own documented remediation (set GOLEDGER_WALLET_PASSPHRASE) silently does NOT seal an already-created plaintext wallet (KEY-2, medium), and the public key in the file is unauthenticated and trusted over the private key (KEY-5, low). Two more: the persisted payment-block counter is poisoned permanently by one bad/malicious height report or a documented re-genesis (KEY-3, medium), and reassignment (mint) votes still resolve the typed name to a key via the untrusted node, so a validator signs a certificate targeting a key they never saw (KEY-4, medium) — the same class that was fixed for the payment path but left in the mint path. All five are traced end-to-end with failing PoC tests.

findings.title: DNS-rebinding bypasses the CSRF/origin guard — drive-by signed payments and governance votes with the local key
findings.description: sameOrigin() only checks that Sec-Fetch-Site is not cross/same-site and that Origin.Host == r.Host — it never compares against a FIXED expected host (e.g. 127.0.0.1:<listen>). Under a DNS-rebinding attack the victim loads http://evil.example:8090 (attacker IP), the attacker re-points the name to 127.0.0.1, and the page fetches /send. The browser now sees page-origin and request-URL as the SAME origin, sending Origin: http://evil.example:8090, Host: evil.example:8090, Sec-Fetch-Site: same-origin — all of which the guard accepts (Origin.Host==r.Host holds by construction; same-origin is the trusted branch). The wallet, which auto-signs with the local key and listens on localhost, then signs and submits whatever the page asks. The deliberate no-header 'curl' fallback (returns true) is a second, independent bypass for any non-browser client that can reach the port. The prior CSRF HIGH (#27) is recorded fixed; this is a concrete bypass of that fix still present in current code.
findings.failure_scenario: User runs the wallet (and, for governance, is a validator) and, while it runs, visits an attacker page. The page rebinds its hostname to 127.0.0.1:8090, reads GET / same-origin (balance, public key), then POSTs /send (pay the attacker) and /admin/reassignment (mint to the attacker via a ⅔ vote). PoC drives the real handlers through the real guard with Origin/Host = the rebound name and Sec-Fetch-Site: same-origin; the node receives a VALID wallet-signed payment and a VALID reassignment vote.
findings.attacker: a web page the user visits (while the wallet runs)
findings.known_status: new — the CSRF guard (#27 / findings 'External review G1') is recorded as fixed and is tested only against classic cross-site/same-site/foreign-Origin and the curl fallback; DNS rebinding (same Origin==Host after rebind) was never in the test table and bypasses the fix.
findings.poc: <scratch>/wallet-ui/ui/poc_rebind_test.go (TestPoCDNSRebindingBypassesGuard) — FAILS: logs 'BYPASS: node received a VALID payment signed by the wallet key ... amount=999' and a VALID reassignment vote 'set ... to 1000000', plus rebound GET / serving the wallet page+key.
findings.fix: Bind the guard to a fixed expected authority: reject any request whose Host header is not the configured -listen host:port (or an explicit allowlist), independently of Origin, and additionally require Origin/Referer to equal that same fixed value when present. Keep the server on 127.0.0.1. Consider dropping the blanket no-header allow in favor of a localhost-only + fixed-Host check; if a no-browser escape hatch is kept for curl, gate it behind a loopback-peer check. Set X-Frame-Options/CSP frame-ancestors 'none' as defense-in-depth.

findings.title: Setting GOLEDGER_WALLET_PASSPHRASE as instructed does NOT seal an existing plaintext wallet — key stays in plaintext, silently
findings.description: On a non-interactive first run the wallet stores the Ed25519 private key in base64 PLAINTEXT and warns 'Set GOLEDGER_WALLET_PASSPHRASE to seal it' (keyfile.go:236); README repeats 'Set it ... to keep the key sealed'. But the plaintext→sealed upgrade is gated by `interactive() && os.Getenv(passphraseEnv) == ""` (keyfile.go:90): when the operator follows the advice and sets the env var, the upgrade branch is skipped and the file is left plaintext — and because the run is now non-interactive with the var set, no further warning is emitted on any later start. The env var only ever seals a FRESH key (newPassphrase at creation); it never seals an already-created plaintext one. So the documented remediation is a silent no-op, leaving a validator/governance key readable by anyone who can read the file or a backup.
findings.failure_scenario: Operator runs the wallet as a service once without the var (plaintext + warning), reads the warning, sets GOLEDGER_WALLET_PASSPHRASE in the unit, restarts. PoC: create wallet with empty env (plaintext), set env to a passphrase, reload — wallet.json still has privateKey in plaintext (Encrypted==nil). Operator believes the key is sealed; it is not.
findings.attacker: local user on the machine, or anyone who obtains a backup/disk image of wallet.json
findings.known_status: new — findings 'Third pass' records the sealing feature and the env var for services as the fix for plaintext storage; the gap that the env var does not upgrade an existing plaintext file (and suppresses the warning thereafter) is not recorded.
findings.poc: <scratch>/wallet-ui/ui/poc_keyfile_test.go (TestPoCEnvPassphraseDoesNotSealExistingPlaintext) — FAILS: 'after setting GOLEDGER_WALLET_PASSPHRASE as instructed, the wallet file still holds the private key in PLAINTEXT'.
findings.fix: When a plaintext key loads and a passphrase is available (env var OR interactive), re-seal in place and rewrite the file atomically — drop the `os.Getenv(passphraseEnv) == ""` condition from the upgrade gate. At minimum, keep printing the 'stored UNENCRYPTED' warning on every start while the on-disk form is plaintext, even when the env var is set, so the operator is not misled.

findings.title: Persisted payment-block counter is poisoned permanently by one bad/malicious height, and survives a documented re-genesis — payments then never land
findings.description: nextPaymentBlockID = max(height()+lookahead, lastPaymentBlockID+1), then persists the result to <wallet>.state. height() trusts the node's /hdls/status with no sanity bound, and the persisted counter is monotonic and NOT scoped to a network/genesis. One out-of-range height — a dishonest or buggy reference node reporting a huge value, or simply the OLD chain's height carried across a documented re-genesis (migration restarts at height 1, but the manual tells users to copy wallet.json AND wallet.json.state together) — latches lastPaymentBlockID to that large value forever. Every later payment, even against an honest node and across restarts, then names a far-future BlockID. The node accepts it (admitPayment only rejects BlockID < height, node/node.go:436) and signs a receipt, but the payment waits for a block that effectively never arrives (mempool.dropBelow only evicts past blocks), so it never commits: a 'receipt but money never moved' outcome the user cannot clear.
findings.failure_scenario: PoC: node reports height 2^40 once; wallet signs one payment (persists 2^40). Node then reports honest height 10; after restart the wallet still names block 1099511627780 — every future payment is unspendable. Re-genesis variant needs no attacker: after a migration to height 1, a wallet whose .state holds 5000 names block 5001+ and cannot pay on the new chain until it reaches 5001.
findings.attacker: the wallet's reference node (one bad /hdls/status), or no attacker at all (a documented re-genesis / chain reset)
findings.known_status: materially worse than #29 (height() returns 0 on node error, accepted as benign). Here a non-zero out-of-range height is PERSISTED and poisons all future payments across restarts and across a switch to honest infrastructure; the re-genesis interaction (with the manual's copy-both-files guidance) gives a no-attacker trigger.
findings.poc: <scratch>/wallet-ui/ui/poc_blockid_test.go (TestPoCPersistedBlockIDCounterUnbounded) — FAILS: 'with the honest tip at height 10 the next payment names block 1099511627780'.
findings.fix: Clamp/sanity-check height(): ignore a status height that is wildly beyond the last observed one, and never let a single report jump the counter by more than a bounded window. Scope the .state file to (networkID, genesis digest) so it resets on a new chain. Cap nextPaymentBlockID at height()+lookahead+small-slack and detect/log when the persisted counter is far ahead of the live tip.

findings.title: Admin reassignment (mint) votes resolve the typed name to a key via the untrusted node — validator signs a certificate targeting a key it never saw
findings.description: VoteReassignment maps the operator's typed name to a key with resolveAccountKey, which trusts whatever /hdls/accounts returns, and binds PreviousAmount from balanceOf (same untrusted source). It then signs the reassignment vote over the node-supplied Account key and PreviousAmount without ever showing the resolved key to the operator or checking it is a key they intended. A malicious/compromised reference node returns a fabricated account {Name:'coop', PublicKey: attacker, Amount: X}; the validator, intending to vote 'coop', signs a certificate targeting the attacker's key with a node-chosen previous amount. Because reassignment is the MINT path, if ≥⅔ of validators share that node (plausible when a village points every wallet at the founder's node) the quorum forms on the attacker's key and mints to it. The payment path was explicitly hardened (payments sign the NAME and nodes resolve on-chain — findings 'Third pass') to kill exactly this node-remap vector; the mint path was left resolving client-side, guarded only by the comment's assumption that every validator uses an independent honest node.
findings.failure_scenario: PoC: a node whose /hdls/accounts maps 'coop'→attackerKey. Operator calls VoteReassignment('coop','1000000'); the submitted vote has Account == attackerKey and PreviousAmount == the node's fabricated 7. The UI showed/accepted only the name 'coop'. With a shared/compromised reference node across a ⅔ validator set, the mint enacts.
findings.attacker: the wallet's reference node (a single dishonest/compromised node, amplified if validators share it)
findings.known_status: new angle on an accepted design (admin.go:151-155 comment argues the ⅔/independent-node quorum makes this safe). The new angle: the identical node-remap class was fixed for payments but remains in the reassignment/mint path, the UI never surfaces the resolved key before signing, and the 'independent honest node per validator' premise fails for the common shared-node village deployment.
findings.poc: <scratch>/wallet-ui/ui/poc_admin_test.go (TestPoCReassignmentVoteTargetsNodeChosenKey — FAILS: 'user typed "coop" but signed a reassignment vote targeting the node-supplied attacker key'; also TestPoCReassignmentVoteSignsUnresolvedNameLiterally for the unregistered-name case).
findings.fix: Do not let the node choose the target key for a signed mint vote. Require the operator to enter/confirm a raw public key for reassignment (or display the resolved key + current balance and require explicit confirmation before signing), and/or resolve names on-chain the way payments do. At minimum refuse to sign when resolveAccountKey falls through to a non-key literal.

findings.title: Wallet trusts the stored publicKey over the private key; GCM uses empty associated data (KDF params / version / pubkey unauthenticated)
findings.description: sealPrivateKey calls gcm.Seal(nil, nonce, priv, nil) — empty associated data — so none of the surrounding fields are authenticated: KDF name, Iterations, Salt, and especially the plaintext publicKey live outside the AEAD. loadOrCreateKey decodes k.PublicKey and uses it as the wallet identity WITHOUT deriving/checking it against the private key (an Ed25519 private key embeds its public key, so this is checkable). A tampered or corrupted publicKey field therefore yields a wallet whose displayed 'your account' / receive-address and whose PublicKeyFrom on outgoing payments is a substituted key, with no error at load. The manual tells users a sealed backup is 'safe to store anywhere', implying integrity as well as confidentiality, which the format does not provide for the public part.
findings.failure_scenario: An attacker who can get the victim to restore a tampered (but still sealed) backup flips publicKey to the attacker's own key. The wallet shows and the victim shares the attacker's key as their receive address, so inbound payments are misdirected to the attacker. (Outgoing payments then fail node verification — a loud signal — which bounds stealth; a bit-flip in publicKey from disk corruption produces the same silent wrong-identity with no attacker.)
findings.attacker: holder of a stolen/tampered backup the victim later restores, or no attacker (file corruption of the unauthenticated field)
findings.known_status: new — the brief asks about GCM associated-data binding; findings records the sealing feature but not that KDF params/pubkey are outside the AEAD or that the stored pubkey is trusted over the private key.
findings.poc: <scratch>/wallet-ui/ui/poc_keyfile_test.go (TestPoCPublicKeyNotBoundToPrivateKey) — FAILS: 'a key file whose publicKey does not match its private key loaded without error; wallet identity is now ...'.
findings.fix: Derive the public key from the decrypted Ed25519 private key and either ignore the stored publicKey or verify equality and error on mismatch. Bind version + KDF params (kdf name, iterations, salt) and the public key into the GCM associated data so tampering any of them fails Open. Correct the 'safe to store anywhere' wording to note integrity of the public header is not cryptographically protected.

area: flake-suite — TestPaymentGossipReceiptAndReplay root-cause + full-suite -race runs (node liveness)
summary: TestPaymentGossipReceiptAndReplay is NOT a test-timing artifact. It reliably detects a real node liveness bug: a block proposal that arrives in the post-commit window — after commit(H) increments the height but before startHeight(H+1) builds the new driver (the MinBlockInterval gap) — is authenticated against the OLD height's proposer schedule, dropped, and never re-processed. The height's first proposal attempt is simply lost; recovery waits for the proposer's next reGossipProposal tick (every cfg.Timeout: 5s in the test, default 3s in production). When ≥2 of 4 nodes hit the window the whole height stalls ~one step-timeout, and the test fails when enough heights stall to blow the 20s deadline. A deterministic PoC (one hand-driven node, no reliance on scheduling) reproduces the drop with a >1s margin, and a throughput PoC shows an all-honest, zero-loss 4-validator LAN commits only ~25% of the blocks it should, spending ~2/3 of wall time stalled. A second, independent defect (timeouts are not height-scoped: a propose timer armed at height H fires into height H+1's driver and prevotes nil prematurely) adds variance and rejects timely proposals. A third, unauthenticated defect surfaced while tracing: the proposal signature does not cover the block body, and onProposal records/relays/re-gossips the first-seen authentic-signature copy even when its body fails ApplyBlock, then dedups every genuine copy — so one keyless swapped-body copy delivered first poisons a node's view of the round. A prototype fix (height-scoped timeouts + hold-and-replay the window proposal into the new driver) takes the same network to ~100% of ideal throughput and keeps the whole suite -race green. The full suite (no -short) ran twice under -race with GOLEDGER_CHAOS_SLACK=4 plus the ui module under -race: all green, no data races, no fork/supply violations.

findings.title: Block proposal arriving in the post-commit window is dropped and the height's first round is lost
findings.description: commit() does n.height++ then schedules startHeight(H+1) one MinBlockInterval later (node.go:656,678). In that window the new driver does not exist yet, but n.driver still points at the decided height-H driver. onProposal (node.go:495) requires n.driver!=nil and checks p.Proposer against n.driver.Proposer(round), which uses the OLD height; for H+1's proposal that is the wrong proposer (or, when consecutive proposers coincide, it is fed to the decided driver and then dedups every genuine copy). Either way the proposal is dropped, not relayed, and never re-processed. startHeight(H+1) builds a fresh driver with no proposal. The only recovery is the proposer's reGossipProposal every cfg.Timeout (sync.go:67). When >=2 of 4 nodes hit the window the height needs no quorum and stalls ~one step-timeout.
findings.failure_scenario: 4 equal validators, localhost, no loss. N commits H at t, sets height=H+1, schedules startHeight at t+300ms. H+1's proposer broadcasts at ~its own t+300ms; the copy lands on N at ~t+312ms, before N's startHeight runs. onProposal checks it against the height-H schedule -> wrong proposer -> dropped, not relayed. N then starts H+1 with no proposal and cannot prevote. If a second node also dropped it, <3 nodes hold the proposal, so round 0 cannot reach quorum; every node waits ~cfg.Timeout for reGossipProposal, then commits at round 0/1 that many seconds late. Enough such heights before block 5 blow the test's 20s deadline (observed 5.6/10.6/15.9/20.0s).
findings.attacker: no attacker (bug; normal operation, no faults needed)
findings.known_status: new — not in findings.md/TODO.md. Distinct from the 2026-07-31 'duplicate proposal re-relayed unverified' fix and from the vote/proposal re-gossip work (TODO 'Vote re-gossip'), which masks this by eventually re-sending; the first attempt is still always lost in the window.
findings.poc: <scratch>/flake-suite/node/flake_poc_test.go (TestPoCDeadWindowProposalDropped, TestPoCDeadWindowProposalHeldNeverProcessed — both FAIL, print the dropped/held proposal) and flake-suite/node/flake_throughput_poc_test.go (TestPoCThroughput3Validators/4Validators — FAIL: ~17-31 of ~104 ideal heights, ~8s/12s stalled). Prototype fix in /tmp/.../scratchpad/flake-suite-fix makes both PASS (105-111/104) and keeps the whole -race suite green.
findings.fix: In commit() set n.driver=nil after the height advances, and in onProposal handle n.driver==nil during the window: authenticate against the NEW height's schedule (validatorsFor(n.accounts).ProposerAt(p.Height,p.Round)) and buffer the proposal in heightProposals; then have startHeight replay the buffered proposals (and heightVotes) into the freshly-built driver. See flake-suite-fix/node/node.go.

findings.title: Consensus timeouts are not height-scoped: a stale timer fires into a later height's driver
findings.description: arm() (node.go:599) posts event{kind:evTimeout, step, round} carrying no height, and the handler (node.go:274) feeds it to whatever n.driver currently is as long as n.driver!=nil. The driver only guards round!=d.round (driver.go:233), and round numbers restart each height, so a propose/prevote timer armed at height H (e.g. round 0) fires into height H+1's brand-new driver (also round 0) after the height advanced. The node then prevotes nil far earlier than its own H+1 propose timeout is due, and rejects a valid, timely H+1 proposal that arrives within the intended window. Impact is bounded (one burned round, self-healing) but it compounds LIVE-1 and independently costs rounds whenever fan-out latency is a meaningful fraction of the step timeout — the documented multi-hop / slow-LAN case.
findings.failure_scenario: cfg.Timeout=1s, MinBlockInterval small. Node arms (propose, round 0) for height H at t (due t+1s). Height H commits and H+1 starts at t+0.68s. At t+1s the height-H timer fires; the handler feeds it to the height-H+1 driver (round 0, propose step) and the node prevotes NIL, though its own height-H+1 propose timeout is not due until ~t+1.68s. A valid height-H+1 proposal delivered at ~t+1.1s (0.42s into a 1s budget) is then refused, burning round 0.
findings.attacker: no attacker (bug)
findings.known_status: new — not recorded in findings.md/TODO.md.
findings.poc: <scratch>/flake-suite/node/flake_poc_test.go (TestPoCStaleTimeoutFiresIntoLaterHeight — FAIL, prints the premature nil prevote) and flake-suite/node/flake_staletimer_poc_test.go (TestPoCStaleTimersUnderSlowFanout — measurement: pristine ~30 heights with round>=1 occurrences vs ~55 clean under the full fix). Height-scoping the timer (flake-suite-fix) removes the premature prevote.
findings.fix: Tag each armed timer with the current height (arm captures n.height) and drop the evTimeout in handle() unless e.height==n.height, as the catch-up/commit guards already do for messages.

findings.title: Swapped-body proposal under a genuine signature poisons a round (signature does not cover the block body)
findings.description: proposalSignFields (messages.go:155) signs height/round/validRound/StateDigest but NOT the block body. onProposal accepts the first copy whose signature verifies and whose p.Proposer is the scheduled proposer (node.go:507), stores p.Block under its StateDigest and remembers/relays it even when ApplyBlock says the body is invalid (node.go:510-513) — the held fast path (node.go:498) and relay dedup (relay.go:29) then key only on StateDigest, so every later genuine copy is discarded. Because the signature omits the body, a 'genuinely invalid block the proposer signed' and 'a swapped body under a copied signature' are indistinguishable. Any peer/relay (no key, not a validator) can replay a seen proposal with a swapped body; if its copy arrives first the node prevotes nil against the real block, re-floods the forgery every cfg.Timeout, ignores genuine copies, and can only advance via height catch-up.
findings.failure_scenario: N1 proposes a valid block B for height H (digest D, signature S over D). A keyless observer that saw it re-sends ProposalMsg{same H,R,VR,Proposer=N1,Signature=S, Block=forged body, StateDigest=D}. VerifyProposal passes (body not signed). It reaches honest node N first: N runs ApplyBlock(forged)->invalid, stores forged under D, remembers it, relays it, feeds the driver Valid=false -> N prevotes nil. The 4 genuine copies that follow hit the held/relay dedup on D and are dropped. Even after 3/4 validators precommit B, N's stored proposal is Valid=false so it never decides H via consensus; it stalls until checkpoint catch-up. On a multi-hop topology a relay node can forward only the forged copy, spreading the stall.
findings.attacker: anyone reaching the port / a gossip peer (no key, no validator slot)
findings.known_status: new angle on a findings.md item recorded as FIXED. The 2026-07-31 RC review fixed 'a duplicate proposal re-relayed unverified' by making the held-proposal fast path never relay a duplicate; that closed the proposer-refloods-a-copied-digest path. It did NOT address the FIRST-sight copy: an invalid-body proposal under a genuine signature is still recorded, relayed, re-gossiped, and used to dedup the genuine block. Materially new: keyless, poisons the round rather than merely re-flooding.
findings.poc: <scratch>/flake-suite/node/flake_swapbody_poc_test.go (TestPoCSwappedBodyFirstSightPoisonsRound — FAIL: node prevotes nil against the valid block, relays the forgery, ignores 4 genuine copies, stays at the height though 3/4 precommitted).
findings.fix: Bind the block body into the proposal signature (add StateDigest's preimage or a body hash to proposalSignFields), so a swapped body fails VerifyProposal and is distinguishable from a proposer's own invalid block; or in onProposal refuse to let an ApplyBlock-invalid first copy occupy the round's held/relay slot (verify body->digest before remember/relay). Ties to the owner's 'two signings = burned key' principle: a one-shot signature that under-binds its payload lets a forgery through with no second signing to detect.

findings.title: Docs claim healthy-network cadence and self-heal that the proposal-window drop contradicts
findings.description: docs/consensus.md and docs/governance.md describe timeouts as a fallback for an unreliable network ('under an unreliable network the rounds eventually stretch past message latency'), implying a healthy network commits at the block-interval cadence. In fact LIVE-1 makes an all-honest, zero-loss network lose round 0 of most heights to the post-commit-window drop and wait ~one step-timeout (default 3s) for reGossipProposal on the majority of blocks — a ~4x throughput shortfall with no faults. security.md:106 frames periodic re-gossip purely as partition self-heal; it is in fact the routine recovery path that masks the window bug every height. The claims are not false in principle but materially overstate steady-state liveness; worth correcting alongside the LIVE-1 fix (after which the cadence claim holds).
findings.failure_scenario: An operator reads docs/governance.md's timing-profile section, sets minBlockIntervalMs=1000/timeoutMs=3000 as documented, and expects ~1 block/s on a healthy LAN. The network instead produces roughly one block per ~3s because nearly every height burns round 0 in the window and waits for reGossipProposal — contradicting the documented expectation, with no fault present.
findings.attacker: no attacker (documentation vs behaviour)
findings.known_status: new — the docs do not mention the post-commit-window drop; this surfaces with LIVE-1.
findings.poc: <scratch>/flake-suite/node/flake_throughput_poc_test.go (ideal vs actual height counts quantify the cadence gap).
findings.fix: Either fix LIVE-1 (then the cadence claim is accurate) or note in docs/consensus.md and docs/operating-a-network.md that current steady-state block time is governed by the step timeout, not the block interval, until the window drop is addressed.

notes:
ROOT CAUSE (verdict: real node liveness bug, not a timing artifact). The payment in the test names BlockID = h+3 (h=2) => block 5, so the network must reach height 5 within the 20s (xslack) deadline. Instrumented trace of the real 4-node HTTP stack (GOLEDGER_TRACE in /tmp/.../scratchpad/flake-suite-trace; captured slow/failing traces in /tmp/.../scratchpad/flake-suite-logs/traces) shows the exact sequence at every slow/failed run:
  1. Node commits height H (commit(): n.height++ then time.AfterFunc(MinBlockInterval, evNextHeight); node.go:656,678). The decided height-H driver is still installed as n.driver.
  2. Height H+1's scheduled proposer also waited its own MinBlockInterval, so its proposal lands on peers at ~the same moment their startHeight(H+1) is due — a race. When the proposal wins the race it is in the 'post-commit window'.
  3. onProposal (node.go:495,507) checks p.Proposer against n.driver.Proposer(round) — the OLD height-H driver. For H+1 the scheduled proposer differs (4 equal validators: round-robin, consecutive proposers differ ~99.8% of the time), so the check fails: 'proposal DROPPED wrong-proposer/bad-sig ... expected(driver h=H)=...'. The proposal is NOT relayed and NOT buffered.
  4. startHeight(H+1) then builds a fresh driver with heldVotes but heldProposals empty; the node cannot prevote. Genuine re-sends are dedup-dropped (held fast path / relaySeen, keyed on digest) until reGossipProposal re-floods on the cfg.Timeout cadence (5s in the test). With >=2 of 4 nodes having dropped it, <3 hold the proposal => round 0 cannot reach the 3-of-4 quorum => the WHOLE height waits ~5s (then commits at round 0, or at round 1 after the growing timeout). Traces show commits landing at round 1 after 15s.
  5. Stacked across heights 2->5, each poisoned height costs ~one step timeout; 3-4 poisoned heights = 15-20s, tripping the deadline. Observed durations (40-run traced loop): bimodal at ~1.9s (no height hit the window) and 5.6/6.2/10.6/11.3/15.6/15.9/16.6/18.6/20.0s (1..4 heights poisoned); 5 of 40 exceeded 20s and FAILED with exactly 'payment submitted to one node did not gossip and commit across a quorum'. This matches the owner-reported 2s-usual / 15.7s-once / 20s-fail profile precisely, and is independent of machine load (the deterministic single-node PoCs reproduce the drop with >1s margins while the box was busy with concurrent reviewers).
  A second, independent defect amplifies it: timeouts are not height-scoped (LIVE-2). A propose/prevote timer armed at height H fires into height H+1's new driver (round numbers restart), causing premature nil prevotes that burn additional rounds; traces show 'TIMEOUT step=0 round=0 (driver round 0 step 1)' arriving right after a height change.
  A third defect surfaced while tracing the drop logic (LIVE-3): the proposal signature omits the block body, so onProposal's first-sight record+relay of an invalid body lets a keyless swapped-body copy poison a round. Not the flake's cause but the same subsystem and directly on-theme for the eMudhra 'two signings = burned key' review (a one-shot signature that under-binds its payload needs no second signing to forge).

The single necessary-and-sufficient fix for the flake is LIVE-1 (buffer the window proposal and replay it into the new driver); LIVE-2's height-scoping removes the remaining variance. Prototype in /tmp/.../scratchpad/flake-suite-fix (diff at /tmp/.../scratchpad/flake-suite-logs/fix-node.go.diff): flake test 30x short + 15x short, all <2s; throughput PoC 105-111 of ~104 ideal heights (was ~17-31); full node package under -race + GOLEDGER_CHAOS_SLACK=4 green. The fix touches only the node layer (no ledger/consensus digest or signature change), so it is not a wire-format break.
